sections.title: Exponential coordinates for rigid motion and twists
Screws: a geometric description of twists

scenes.title: Screw story
scenes.brief: A slate timeline strip with two portrait-free markers (a 🔩 and a 🔧). Beat 1: a blue box jumps between two random poses; a gold helix axis appears and a ghost box slides+spins along it to join them (Chasles). Beat 2: scatter several teal force arrows on the box; they merge into one purple line with a force arrow and a twirl arrow on it (Poinsot). Beat 3: the two pictures sit side by side in matching shapes — the twist helix and the wrench helix — to say they are mirror ideas. Beat 4: drag the box’s orientation on a sphere; Euler-angle dials jam at a coral pole while a screw readout stays smooth.

scenes.title: Frozen distances
scenes.brief: A blue body made of teal dots joined by springs-that-cannot-stretch. Drag/rotate the body: every pairwise distance readout stays frozen (lime). A draggable teal arrow slides around the body without changing (free vector). A mirror toggle flips z: distances still lime but the attached right-hand frame turns into a left hand and flashes coral. Final beat: hide all dots except one origin + red/green/blue triad; dragging the triad alone reproduces where every dot goes.

scenes.title: Rotation matrix
scenes.brief: Fixed slate frame A and a blue body frame B sharing an origin. Drag B on a trackball; its red/green/blue axes are copied live as the three columns of a 3×3 grid whose cells are colored by the axis they came from. Readouts: column lengths (all 1), pairwise dot products (all 0) and det (+1) glow lime. A pink point q fixed in B shows q_b (body numbers, constant) and q_a = R q_b (spatial numbers, changing). A third frame C chains on B; R_ac = R_ab R_bc is computed and the chained frame matches. A hat panel turns any orange vector a into a 3×3 skew grid and shows a×b = â b with matching arrows.

scenes.title: Spin = exp
scenes.brief: An orange axis arrow ω (drag its tip on a sphere) through the origin and a blue link with a pink tip q. Slider θ spins the link; q traces a pink circle around ω, its velocity arrow is ω×q (always tangent). A “tiny steps” slider n chops θ into n straight nudges (I + ω̂θ/n)ⁿ whose ghost path converges to the circle. Rodrigues panel: three colored matrices I, sinθ·ω̂, (1−cosθ)·ω̂² added live, sum equals the series. Inverse mode: drag a random gold target frame; the trace gives θ, the skew part gives ω, and the reconstructed orange axis snaps onto the right line; at R = I the axis spins freely (coral “any axis” flash).

scenes.title: Euler angles
scenes.brief: A gimbal of three orange rings (z, then new y, then new z) holding a blue body. Three dials α, β, γ; each turn animates about the CURRENT body axis. Matrix panel shows Rz(α)Ry(β)Rz(γ) computed live. Inverse mode: drag the body; atan2 recovers the three dials; when β→0 two rings line up, α and γ merge into one coral “α+γ” dial and a ghost family of (α,0,−α) all give the same pose. ZYX toggle moves the lock to pitch = ±90°. A globe beat: try to comb a hairy sphere flat — a cowlick always remains.

scenes.title: Quaternions
scenes.brief: A 4-bar meter (q0 white-ish slate, q1 red, q2 green, q3 blue) whose squared lengths always sum to 1 (lime ring). Drag a body on a trackball; the bars update from cos(θ/2), ω sin(θ/2). Product panel: two quaternions P, Q multiply via (scalar: q0p0 − q·p, vector: q0p + p0q + q×p), each term drawn as an arrow; swapping order changes only the cross-product arrow (coral). Half-angle beat: spin the body 360° — the body is back but Q has become −Q; spin 720° to return Q (belt-trick ribbon). Compose two rotations and see Q_ac = Q_ab·Q_bc drive the same pose as R_ab R_bc.

scenes.title: Homogeneous g
scenes.brief: Slate world frame A and a blue body frame B with a pink point q. Drag B’s origin (teal p_ab arrow) and twist its orientation; a 4×4 grid shows [R p; 0 1] with the rotation block colored per axis and the p column teal. Point/vector toggle: a point carries a trailing 1 and is moved by translation; a vector carries a 0 and ignores it (two arrows, one shifts, one does not). Chain a third frame C: ḡ_ac = ḡ_ab ḡ_bc lights up. Inverse button flips the arrow from B back to A with −Rᵀp. Example: a door swinging on a hinge at distance l₁ along y.

scenes.title: Twist = exp
scenes.brief: Two toy joints side by side: an orange revolute hinge (axis ω through point q) and an orange prismatic slider (direction v). The pink tip’s velocity arrow is ω×(p−q) or v. A 4×4 ξ̂ = [ω̂ v; 0 0] grid and a 6-bar ξ = (v, ω) meter (v teal, ω orange) update as you drag the axis. Slider θ: the body flows along exp(ξ̂θ) — n tiny steps converge on the smooth helix. Log mode: drag a gold target pose; the scene finds ω, θ from the rotation and solves A v = p for v, then the orange axis appears and flowing along it lands exactly on the target. Absolute vs relative toggle shows why measuring from the start pose gives the tidy twist.

scenes.title: Screw motion
beats: 🎯 Chasles: every move is a screw
scenes.brief: A blue bolt-shaped body on a gold axis line l (drag point q and direction ω). Sliders: pitch h and magnitude θ; the body spins θ and advances hθ along l, leaving a pink helix. Readouts h = ωᵀv/‖ω‖², q* = ω×v/‖ω‖², M. Twist mode: edit ξ = (v, ω) bars and the screw axis/pitch redraw. Chasles mode: drop two random poses of the body; the scene computes the one screw that joins them and plays it. Pitch 0 shows a hinge; pitch ∞ (ω = 0) shows a slider.

scenes.title: Spin rate ω
scenes.brief: A blue body spins about the slate origin under an orange angular-velocity handle. Left panel: the 9 numbers of Ṙ flicker (too many); the products ṘRᵀ and RᵀṘ are drawn as 3×3 grids that are always skew (mirror cells lime/coral). Vee turns them into two orange arrows: ωˢ drawn in the slate world frame and ωᵇ drawn in the blue body frame — the same physical spin axis, different numbers (ωˢ = R ωᵇ). Pink points on the body carry velocity arrows ω×q; a body-camera toggle shows the same arrows as ωᵇ × q_b. Example: a one-joint arm swinging about z shows ωˢ = ωᵇ = (0,0,θ̇).

scenes.title: Twist velocity
beats: 🔩 a screw’s velocity is its twist
scenes.brief: A moving blue body (driven by orange joint dials or a drag handle) with velocity arrows on many pink points. Spatial panel: ġg⁻¹ as a 4×4 twist grid and a 6-bar Vˢ = (vˢ, ωˢ). A translucent ghost extension of the body reaches the slate world origin; the ghost point sitting at the origin shows a teal arrow that equals vˢ (which differs from how fast the body’s own origin moves!). Body panel: g⁻¹ġ and a 6-bar Vᵇ; riding a camera on the body, vᵇ is the body-origin velocity in body axes. The instantaneous screw of Vˢ is drawn as a gold axis with pitch. Screw-motion beat: a constant twist ξ drives the body and Vˢ stays exactly ξθ̇ while Vᵇ = Ad⁻¹ ξθ̇.

scenes.title: Adjoint swap
scenes.brief: One physical gold screw axis (a twist) drawn in 3D; two observer frames (slate A, blue B) placed by dragging. Each observer shows its own 6-bar coordinates of the same twist; a 6×6 Ad_g grid ([R p̂R; 0 R], with the coupling block p̂R in teal) maps one bar set to the other, and the lime “same axis” check confirms the physical screw is unchanged. Chain beat: three frames A→B→C with joint dials; Vˢ_ac = Vˢ_ab + Ad_{g_ab}Vˢ_bc drawn as two summed twist arrows. Two-link arm: each joint contributes a column scaled by θ̇ᵢ (a preview of the spatial Jacobian). Move-the-axis beat: drag a rigid motion g on a joint and watch its twist become Ad_g ξ = g ξ̂ g⁻¹.

scenes.title: Wrench
scenes.brief: A blue object with a teal contact frame B where a purple force arrow f and a curled purple torque τ are applied (drag the arrow). A 6-bar F = (f, τ). Work meter: animate a twist V on the object and a power gauge shows V·F = v·f + ω·τ, integrated into a work bar. Shift beat: drag the reference frame C elsewhere; the equivalent wrench Fc = Adᵀ F_b is redrawn at C — same force, extra torque −p×f (coral) — and the work gauge is unchanged for every test twist. Sum beat: several finger pushes are each moved to the object frame O and then added. Grasp preview: two fingers S1, S2 on an object, net wrench on O shown as one arrow pair.

scenes.title: Poinsot screw
beats: 🪛 push along + twist about a line
scenes.brief: A slate world frame and a blue body. Draw a gold screw line l (point q, direction ω), pitch h and magnitude M: a purple force of size M along l and a purple torque hM about l are applied, and the 6-bar F = M(ω, −ω×q + hω) is shown. Poinsot mode: throw several random purple forces/torques on the body; their sum F is reduced to a single gold axis through f×τ/‖f‖² with pitch fᵀτ/‖f‖² — a screwdriver glyph sits on it. Duality beat: the same panel layout as the twist screw scene, colors swapped (orange motion ↔ purple force), highlighting that pitch 0 means pure spin for a twist but pure push for a wrench.

scenes.title: Zero work
scenes.brief: Two gold screw axes S1 (as an orange twist) and S2 (as a purple wrench) in 3D, each with draggable point, direction and pitch. A power gauge shows V·F; the reciprocal product M₁M₂((h₁+h₂)cos α − d sin α) is computed from the drawn distance d (common-normal segment, teal) and angle α; when it hits 0 the pair glows lime “reciprocal”. Constraint beat: three purple finger forces press a blue body (Fig 2.16); the scene computes all twists reciprocal to them and plays those free motions as ghost wiggles in lime; adding forces removes wiggles. A dimension bar r + n always sums to 6.

scenes.title: Chapter 2 Map
scenes.brief: A single summary board: a blue body in a slate world. Five tiles light up one at a time and each re-runs a 5-second loop from its scene: the 4×4 pose grid, the helix flow from a twist, the spatial/body velocity bars linked by Ad, a wrench moved by Adᵀ, and a twist–wrench pair with a zero power gauge. A family-tree strip (📜 1800s → 📚 1900 → 💻 modern matrix treatment) closes the chapter.

scenes.title: Flatland motion
beats: 📍 every move spins about a pole
scenes.brief: Everything in 2D on a slate tabletop: a blue card shape with a red/green frame. Beat 1: the rotation dial is literally a point on the unit circle; the 2×2 grid [cos −sin; sin cos] reads off it. Beat 2: ω̂ = [0 −ω; ω 0] and exp(ω̂θ) via n tiny turns. Beat 3: drop two card poses; a gold pole dot appears and the card spins about it to connect them (or slides if there is no turn). Beat 4: 3-number twists (v_x, v_y, ω), spatial/body velocities, and the 3×3 planar adjoint with its (p_y, −p_x) column.

pages.summary: Chapter opening: rigid motion keeps distances; Chasles (motions are screws) and Poinsot (forces are wrenches) are the two pillars, later unified by Ball and recast here with matrices and exponentials.

atoms.idea: Chapter 2 title: Rigid Body Motion.
A rigid motion keeps every pairwise distance; kinematics, dynamics and control of robots all rest on describing such motions, here with linear algebra plus screw theory.
atoms.feynman: Carry a brick across the room: you can turn it and move it, but no two crumbs of the brick ever get closer or farther apart.
atoms.visual: A blue brick of teal dots with thin lines between every pair; drag/spin it freely and a column of distance readouts never flickers (lime). Try a coral “squish” handle: it refuses to move.

atoms.idea: Chasles (early 1800s): any repositioning of a rigid body can be done as a rotation about one line plus a slide along that same line — a screw motion; its infinitesimal version, the twist, packs linear and angular velocity together.
atoms.feynman: Any way you move a jar lid from one spot to another, you could instead have done it by screwing it along one invisible bolt.
atoms.visual: Two random poses of a blue box (start ghost, gold target). Press ▶: a gold axis line appears and the box spins about it while sliding along it, landing exactly on the target; a pink helix trail marks the path. Re-roll the target: a new axis, always works.

atoms.idea: Poinsot: however many forces act on a rigid body, their combined effect matches that of one push along some line together with a twist about that very line — a wrench, the dual partner of a twist.
atoms.feynman: However many kids push on a merry-go-round from different spots, you could replace them all with one push along a line plus a twist about that line — like one person using a screwdriver.
atoms.visual: Several teal force arrows stuck on the blue box; their sum collapses into one purple line carrying a straight force arrow and a curled torque arrow. Toggle the original forces on/off: the box’s motion is identical either way.

atoms.idea: Ball built a full theory of screws (1900) on Chasles and Poinsot; this book redoes it with homogeneous coordinates and the matrix exponential, which turns a twist into its screw motion, using only basic linear algebra.
atoms.feynman: Two old recipes got collected into one cookbook a century ago; we are rewriting that cookbook using a kitchen gadget (the matrix) everyone already owns.
atoms.visual: A slate timeline: 🔩 (1830) and 🔧 (1804) markers flow into a 📚 (1900) marker, which flows into a 4×4 matrix grid with an “exp” arrow turning a twist bar-chart into a helix.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Why screws: no local-coordinate singularities and clear geometry. Section 2.1 starts: particles as coordinate triples, a rigid body as fixed pairwise distances, rigid motion vs rigid displacement, and the map g(t).

atoms.idea: The abstract matrix Lie group / Lie algebra version of this theory is deferred to Appendix A.
atoms.feynman: The same toy has a grown-up instruction manual in the back of the box.
atoms.visual: A small 📘 icon on the timeline links forward to the appendix map; tapping it shows SO(3)/SE(3) as curved sheets with flat tangent planes so(3)/se(3).

atoms.idea: Two payoffs of screws, twists and wrenches: a global description of motion with no singularities from local coordinates (unlike Euler angles), and a geometric picture that simplifies analysing mechanisms.
atoms.feynman: A map of the Earth always tears somewhere, but a globe never does; screws are the globe.
atoms.visual: Split screen: left, three Euler dials driving the box — drag toward a pole and two dials jam (coral flash); right, the same drag through a screw/exponential readout stays smooth (lime trace).

atoms.idea: Section 2.1 heading: Rigid Body Transformations.
A particle’s position is the triple of its projections onto three orthonormal axes of an inertial frame; its trajectory is a curve p(t) in R³.
atoms.feynman: Where a fly is in a room is three numbers: how far along the floor, across the floor, and up the wall.
atoms.visual: A slate room corner with red/green/blue axes; a teal fly dot moves along a pink curve and drops three dashed projection lines whose lengths are the x, y, z readouts.

atoms.idea: A rigid body is a set of particles whose pairwise distances never change, whatever moves or pushes it: ‖p(t) − q(t)‖ = ‖p(0) − q(0)‖.
atoms.feynman: A Lego brick, not a jelly: tug on it and every stud stays the same distance from every other stud.
atoms.visual: Teal particles on a blue body; pick any two (they glow) and a ruler readout between them; drag the body around — the ruler number is frozen; try a coral pinch handle that would stretch it and it is locked.

atoms.idea: A rigid motion is a continuous distance-preserving movement; its net effect from start to end is a rigid displacement, which in general mixes translation and rotation.
atoms.feynman: A movie of a chair being carried is the motion; the before-and-after photos are the displacement.
atoms.visual: A blue chair animates along a path (motion, with a pink trail); a toggle hides the film and shows only start ghost and end pose joined by one gold arrow (displacement).

atoms.idea: For a body occupying a set O, a rigid motion is a time-indexed family of maps g(t): O → R³ sending each body point’s initial coordinates to its coordinates at time t; a displacement is one such map g. (Continues on next page.)
atoms.feynman: Each crumb on the brick has a name tag; g(t) is the lookup that tells you where the crumb with that tag is at time t.
atoms.visual: Teal dots carry faint ghost copies at their start positions; a time slider t draws thin arrows from every ghost to its current dot — those arrows are g(t) acting on each point.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Points vs free vectors; how a rigid map acts on vectors; distance alone allows mirror images, so Definition 2.1 also demands that cross products be preserved; this implies dot products are preserved too (polarization).

atoms.idea: A rigid displacement is the single map from initial to final configuration (end of the previous sentence).
atoms.feynman: Only the before-and-after photo matters, not the trip.
atoms.visual: Same scene as the previous atom with the time slider pinned at its end: only one set of arrows from ghosts to final dots.

atoms.idea: A vector v = q − p joins two points and has direction and length (Euclidean norm), but no fixed location: any other pair r, s with s − r = q − p gives the same free vector.
atoms.feynman: An arrow that says “three steps north” means the same thing whether you stand in the kitchen or the garden.
atoms.visual: Two teal points p, q joined by a teal arrow; drag a second pair r, s around the body — whenever their difference matches, the arrow snaps on and glows lime: same vector, different place.

atoms.label: g* (vectors)
atoms.idea: A rigid map g moves vectors by moving both endpoints: g*(v) = g(q) − g(p), which is again a difference of points, hence a vector.
atoms.feynman: To move the arrow painted on a box, move the box and look where its tail and head landed.
atoms.visual: Teal arrow from p to q on the blue body; move the body and the arrow is redrawn from g(p) to g(q); a translation-only drag leaves the arrow unchanged, a spin turns it.

atoms.idea: Keeping distances is necessary but not enough: a mirror flip like (x,y,z) ↦ (x,y,−z) keeps all distances yet reverses handedness, which no physical motion can do; so we also require cross products to be preserved.
atoms.feynman: Your reflection in a mirror is exactly your size, but its watch is on the wrong wrist — you can never walk into that pose.
atoms.visual: Mirror toggle on the blue body: every distance readout stays lime, but a right-hand 🤚 glyph on the body becomes a left hand and the z-axis (blue) flips; the cross-product check x×y vs z flashes coral.

atoms.label: Def 2.1
atoms.idea: Definition 2.1: a map g qualifies as a rigid body transformation when it keeps lengths ‖g(p) − g(q)‖ = ‖p − q‖ and keeps cross products intact, g*(v×w) = g*(v) × g*(w).
atoms.feynman: A legal move for a toy must pass two inspections: nothing stretched, and nothing turned inside-out.
atoms.visual: Two lime check lights on the scene: 📏 (all pairwise distances equal) and ✋ (moved x × moved y equals moved z). Normal drags keep both lime; a stretch handle kills 📏, the mirror toggle kills ✋.

atoms.label: polarization
atoms.idea: Consequence: dot products are preserved too, via the polarization identity v₁ᵀv₂ = ¼(‖v₁+v₂‖² − ‖v₁−v₂‖²), which writes the dot product purely in terms of lengths.
atoms.feynman: If you know the lengths of both diagonals of a parallelogram, you know the angle between its sides — and a rigid move keeps those diagonals.
atoms.visual: Two teal arrows v₁, v₂ from one point form a parallelogram; its two diagonals are drawn gold and coral with length readouts; the dot product computed from them matches v₁·v₂ while you rotate the whole picture.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Rigid maps keep dot products, so orthonormal right-handed frames go to orthonormal right-handed frames; a body is tracked by one attached frame. Section 2.2 on rotations begins.

atoms.label: polarization
atoms.idea: Since g* keeps ‖v₁+v₂‖ and ‖v₁−v₂‖, polarization gives v₁ᵀv₂ = g*(v₁)ᵀg*(v₂): angles are kept and perpendicular vectors stay perpendicular.
atoms.feynman: Square corners on a picture frame stay square no matter how you carry it.
atoms.visual: Continue the parallelogram: rotate it and the dot-product readout stays frozen; set v₁ ⟂ v₂ and a little lime right-angle marker stays attached through every move.

atoms.idea: Keeping dot products plus cross products means an orthonormal right-handed frame is sent to an orthonormal right-handed frame.
atoms.feynman: A three-finger salute (thumb, index, middle all at right angles) stays a right-hand salute after any rigid move.
atoms.visual: Red/green/blue triad on the body; after any drag, lime ticks confirm unit length, right angles, and x × y = z.

atoms.idea: Points inside a rigid body may move relative to each other only by rotating, not translating; so the whole body is tracked by one attached Cartesian body frame (position of one point plus orientation), always right-handed (z = x × y).
atoms.feynman: To know where every part of a car is, you only need where the driver’s seat is and which way the car faces.
atoms.visual: Fade the teal dots to ghosts and keep only a body frame (origin + red/green/blue axes). Drag the frame: the ghost dots are reconstructed from the frame and land exactly on the true dots (lime overlap meter 100%).

atoms.idea: Because cross products are kept, a right-handed frame (v₁, v₂, v₃) at p becomes the right-handed frame (g*v₁, g*v₂, g*v₃) at g(p): the motion of the body is exactly the motion of its frame.
atoms.feynman: Glue a little toy compass-and-axes to a box; however you move the box, the toy tells you everything.
atoms.visual: Before/after: ghost triad at p, solid triad at g(p), with thin arrows linking each axis to its image; the handedness check stays lime.

atoms.idea: The rest of the chapter characterises and represents rigid transformations in detail and builds the math used throughout the book.
atoms.feynman: We have decided what moves are allowed; next we build the toolbox for writing them down.
atoms.visual: A chapter map: icons 🧭 (rotation matrix) → 🌀 (exp) → 📦 (4×4 g) → 🔩 (twist/screw) → 🏃 (velocity) → 🔧 (wrench) light up in order.

atoms.idea: Section 2.2 heading: Rotational Motion in R³.
Start with pure rotation: orientation is the relative attitude of a body frame with respect to a fixed frame. (Continues next page.)
atoms.feynman: Before moving the toy around the room, just learn to turn it in your hands.
atoms.visual: Pin the body frame’s origin to the slate world origin so only turning is possible.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.1; the rotation matrix R_ab stacks the body axes (in A coordinates) as columns. Its columns are orthonormal, so RRᵀ = I and det R = ±1, with det = r₁·(r₂×r₃).

atoms.label: Fig 2.1
atoms.idea: Figure 2.1: a body rotating about a fixed point; its dotted body frame axes x_ab, y_ab, z_ab are expressed in the fixed frame, and a point q rides on the body.
atoms.feynman: A globe on a stand: it spins about its centre and a sticker on it shows where a city is.
atoms.visual: Slate frame A and a dotted blue frame B sharing an origin, with a pink point q on B; trackball-drag B.

atoms.idea: Orientation of body frame B relative to inertial frame A: put the A-coordinates of B’s unit axes side by side as columns, R_ab = [x_ab y_ab z_ab]; every rotation gives such a matrix.
atoms.feynman: Write down where the body’s “forward”, “left” and “up” arrows point; those three arrows are the whole answer.
atoms.visual: Drag B; three columns of a 3×3 grid fill live with the red, green and blue axis coordinates (each column tinted with its axis color).

atoms.idea: Subsection 2.2.1 heading: Properties of rotation matrices.

atoms.label: Eq (2.1)
atoms.idea: Each column of R has unit length and is perpendicular to the other two (rᵢᵀrⱼ = 1 if i = j else 0), which is the matrix statement RRᵀ = RᵀR = I.
atoms.feynman: Three sticks of length one, glued at perfect right angles: each sees itself as length 1 and the others as “nothing along me”.
atoms.visual: Beside the grid, a 3×3 table of column dot products: diagonal cells glow lime “1”, off-diagonal glow lime “0”; this table IS RᵀR and stays the identity under any drag.

atoms.idea: From RᵀR = I, det R = ±1; to fix the sign use det R = r₁ᵀ(r₂ × r₃), the signed volume of the box spanned by the columns.
atoms.feynman: The three sticks span a little cube; its volume is +1 for a right hand and −1 for a mirror hand.
atoms.visual: A translucent unit cube spanned by the three columns with its signed volume readout; mirror toggle turns it inside-out and the readout flips to −1 (coral).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Right-handed frames give det R = +1, defining SO(3) and in general SO(n) (Eq 2.2). Group axioms are listed and checked for SO(3); SO(3) is the configuration space of a freely rotating body.

atoms.idea: For a right-handed frame r₂ × r₃ = r₁, so det R = r₁ᵀr₁ = +1; orthogonal matrices with determinant +1 make up SO(3), “special orthogonal”.
atoms.feynman: The right-hand rule means the cube’s volume is always plus one, never minus.
atoms.visual: The signed-volume readout locks to +1 (lime) for every drag; label the set of all reachable grids SO(3).

atoms.label: Eq (2.2)
atoms.idea: SO(n) = {R ∈ Rⁿˣⁿ : RRᵀ = I, det R = +1}; n = 3 is the main case, n = 2 (planar rotations) appears in the exercises.
atoms.feynman: A clock hand turning on a flat face is the 2-D version of the same rule.
atoms.visual: Dimension toggle 2D/3D: in 2D a 2×2 grid with one dial θ; in 3D the trackball 3×3 grid; both show RRᵀ = I and det +1 checks.

atoms.label: group
atoms.idea: A group is a set with an operation satisfying closure, identity, inverses and associativity.
atoms.feynman: Moves on a Rubik’s cube: two moves make a move, “do nothing” is a move, every move can be undone, and grouping doesn’t matter.
atoms.visual: Four badge slots (🔒 closure, 0️⃣ identity, ↩️ inverse, 🔗 associativity) waiting to be lit by the next atom.

atoms.idea: SO(3) is a group: products of rotations are rotations (RRᵀ and det multiply), I is the identity, Rᵀ is the inverse by Eq (2.1), and matrix multiplication is associative. SO(3) is called the rotation group.
atoms.feynman: Turn a book, then turn it again: still just a turn. Turning it back is the same as turning it the opposite way.
atoms.visual: Two orange trackball handles R₁, R₂; the blue body shows R₁R₂ and its checks stay lime (🔒 lights); “undo” applies Rᵀ and the body snaps home (↩️ lights); identity and associativity badges light with tiny demos.

atoms.idea: Each orientation of a freely rotating body corresponds to exactly one R ∈ SO(3), so SO(3) is its configuration space and a motion is a curve R(t).
atoms.feynman: Every way a ball can be turned is one dot on a map of all turnings; spinning the ball draws a line on that map.
atoms.visual: A side panel ball (axis-angle ball of radius π) with a pink dot for the current R; as you drag the body the dot draws a pink curve R(t).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Configuration space defined in general. R_ab converts point coordinates from B to A (q_a = R_ab q_b), acts consistently on vectors, and chains as R_ac = R_ab R_bc (Eq 2.3). Start of the proof that rotations are rigid.

atoms.label: configuration space
atoms.idea: A configuration space Q of a system: each element is a valid configuration and each configuration matches exactly one element.
atoms.feynman: A seating chart where every seat is a real seat and every guest gets exactly one seat.
atoms.visual: The axis-angle ball again: every interior point gives a lime body pose; poses and points are paired one-to-one (antipodal surface points glued, shown by matching colors).

atoms.label: q_a = R_ab q_b
atoms.idea: R_ab also converts coordinates: if q_b are q’s coordinates in B, then q_a = x_ab x_b + y_ab y_b + z_ab z_b = R_ab q_b, a weighted sum of B’s axes written in A.
atoms.feynman: Directions given as “3 steps along the body’s forward, 1 step left” turn into room directions by walking those steps along where forward and left really point.
atoms.visual: Pink point q on the body; its body numbers q_b sit fixed in a blue panel; three colored arrow segments (x_b along red, y_b along green, z_b along blue) chain tip-to-tail to reach q; the slate panel shows q_a = R q_b updating.

atoms.idea: A rotation acts on a vector v_b = q_b − p_b by rotating its endpoints; by linearity the answer is the same for any representing pair of points, so the action is well defined.
atoms.feynman: Rotating a stick by rotating both of its ends gives the same result no matter where on the table the stick lay.
atoms.visual: Two copies of the same teal free vector at different spots on the body; rotate and both images stay parallel and equal (lime equality badge).

atoms.label: Eq (2.3)
atoms.idea: Composition rule: if C has orientation R_bc in B and B has R_ab in A, then R_ac = R_ab R_bc — map from C to B, then from B to A.
atoms.feynman: Directions relayed through a friend: the friend translates your words into theirs, then into mine.
atoms.visual: Three nested frames (slate A, blue B, teal C on B). Drag B and C; the chain product grid R_ab·R_bc equals the measured R_ac grid cell by cell (lime). Swapping the order shows a different, wrong frame in coral.

atoms.idea: Claim to prove: a rotation matrix is a rigid body transformation — it preserves distance and orientation — using cross-product algebra. (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: We now check that turning a toy passes both inspections from Definition 2.1.
atoms.visual: The two inspection lights 📏 and ✋ from the previous scene reappear beside the rotation grid, waiting.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Cross product written as a skew matrix â (Eqs 2.4–2.5). Lemma 2.1: rotations commute with cross products and conjugate hats. Proposition 2.2: rotations preserve distance and orientation.

atoms.label: cross product
atoms.idea: Cross product a × b in components: (a₂b₃ − a₃b₂, a₃b₁ − a₁b₃, a₁b₂ − a₂b₁).
atoms.feynman: Push a door at its edge: the turning it gets depends on how far out and how sideways you push — that sideways-ness is the cross product.
atoms.visual: Two orange arrows a, b; a pink arrow a×b perpendicular to both, length = parallelogram area (shaded); component readouts update as you drag.

atoms.label: Eq (2.4)–(2.5)
atoms.idea: Crossing with a is linear in b, so it is a matrix: the skew-symmetric â (zeros on the diagonal, ±a entries off it), with a × b = â b; â is also written a-hat.
atoms.feynman: A machine that always “crosses with a” is just a fixed recipe of multiplications — write the recipe down once as a grid.
atoms.visual: Drag orange a: a 3×3 grid â fills with 0 diagonal and mirrored ± entries (+ in lime, − in coral); multiplying â by b draws the same pink arrow as a×b.

atoms.label: Lemma 2.1
atoms.idea: Lemma 2.1: for R ∈ SO(3), R(v × w) = (Rv) × (Rw) (Eq 2.6) and R ŵ Rᵀ = (Rw)^ (Eq 2.7).
atoms.feynman: Turning the whole scene of two pencils and their “cross” arrow gives the same as turning the pencils and then building the cross arrow.
atoms.visual: Two paths animate side by side: (cross then rotate) and (rotate then cross); their pink results overlap exactly (lime). A second panel shows R ŵ Rᵀ grid equal to hat(R w).

atoms.idea: Meaning: rotating commutes with crossing; the conjugation rule will later describe how an instantaneous rotation axis is re-expressed in another frame. Proof is direct computation.
atoms.feynman: A spinning top’s axis looks different from a turned camera, but it is the same spin seen from a new angle.
atoms.visual: An orange spin-axis w on the body; turn the camera by R and the axis appears as Rw — the spin seen by the turned camera is R ŵ Rᵀ.

atoms.label: Prop 2.2
atoms.idea: Proposition 2.2: rotation matrices pass both rigidity tests: ‖Rq − Rp‖ = ‖q − p‖ and R(v × w) = Rv × Rw.
atoms.feynman: Turning a toy never stretches it and never mirrors it.
atoms.visual: The 📏 and ✋ lights from Definition 2.1 now switch on lime for every trackball drag of the rotation grid.

atoms.label: Prop 2.2 proof
atoms.idea: Proof: ‖R(q−p)‖² = (q−p)ᵀRᵀR(q−p) = ‖q−p‖² because RᵀR = I; orientation follows from Eq (2.6).
atoms.feynman: A turned ruler is still the same ruler.
atoms.visual: Staircase of two tiles: tile 1 shows the RᵀR block collapsing to I (grid cells fading to identity), leaving ‖q−p‖²; tile 2 replays the Lemma 2.1 overlap.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.2 and exponential coordinates: a point on a body spinning about unit axis ω obeys q̇ = ω × q (Eq 2.8), solved by the matrix exponential, so R(ω, θ) = exp(ω̂θ) (Eq 2.9); ω̂ is skew-symmetric.

atoms.label: Fig 2.2
atoms.idea: Figure 2.2: a point on a link rotating about axis ω traces a circular path from q(0) to q(t).
atoms.feynman: A sticker on a spinning top draws a circle around the top’s stick.
atoms.visual: Orange axis ω through the origin, blue link, pink tip leaving a circular pink trail from its ghost start q(0).

atoms.idea: Subsection 2.2.2 heading: Exponential coordinates for rotation.
Common robotic motion: rotate a body about a unit axis ω by angle θ (radians); we want a formula giving R from the pair (ω, θ).
atoms.feynman: A door: tell me which hinge line and how far to swing it, and I know exactly where the door ends up.
atoms.visual: Drag ω’s tip on a sphere and a θ slider; the body pose is driven only by these two controls.

atoms.label: Eq (2.8)
atoms.idea: At unit spin rate, a body point moves with velocity q̇ = ω × q = ω̂ q: always perpendicular to both the axis and the point.
atoms.feynman: On a merry-go-round you are always pushed sideways, never toward or away from the centre pole.
atoms.visual: Pink velocity arrow on the tip equals ω×q (drawn live); a lime right-angle marker shows it is perpendicular to ω and to the radius.

atoms.label: matrix exponential
atoms.idea: This is a constant linear ODE, so q(t) = exp(ω̂t) q(0) with the matrix exponential I + ω̂t + (ω̂t)²/2! + (ω̂t)³/3! + ….
atoms.feynman: Compound interest: add a tiny bit of growth over and over and you get e; add a tiny bit of turning over and over and you get a rotation.
atoms.visual: Series bar: terms I, ω̂t, (ω̂t)²/2!, … appear one by one as colored ghost tips; each new term moves the predicted tip closer to the true pink tip (error bar in coral shrinks to zero).

atoms.label: Eq (2.9)
atoms.idea: Rotating at unit rate for time θ gives the net rotation R(ω, θ) = exp(ω̂θ).
atoms.feynman: Swing the door at one radian per second for θ seconds and it has turned θ radians.
atoms.visual: θ slider doubles as a stopwatch; the body pose equals exp(ω̂θ) computed live, matrix grid shown.

atoms.idea: ω̂ is skew-symmetric: ω̂ᵀ = −ω̂. (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: Flip the cross-product grid across its diagonal and every entry changes sign.
atoms.visual: The ω̂ grid flips over its diagonal (animated) and every off-diagonal cell swaps between lime + and coral −.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: so(3) (Eq 2.10) is the vector space of skew matrices, identified with R³. The series exp(ω̂θ) (Eq 2.11) collapses, using ω̂² = ωωᵀ − ‖ω‖²I and ω̂³ = −‖ω‖²ω̂ (Lemma 2.3), into Rodrigues’ formula (Eq 2.14); a version for non-unit ω is given.

atoms.label: Eq (2.10)
atoms.idea: so(n) = {S : Sᵀ = −S}, the skew-symmetric matrices; so(3) is a vector space (sums and scalings stay skew) and is identified with R³ via the hat map, which is linear: (v + w)^ = v̂ + ŵ.
atoms.feynman: Spin “instructions” add like arrows: spin a little about x plus a little about y is a spin about the diagonal.
atoms.visual: Two orange axis arrows v and w; their sum v+w and the sum of their hat grids are shown; the hat of the sum matches the sum of the hats cell by cell (lime).

atoms.label: Eq (2.11)
atoms.idea: With ‖ω‖ = 1, write exp(ω̂θ) = I + θω̂ + θ²ω̂²/2! + θ³ω̂³/3! + ….
atoms.feynman: A unit-speed spin, run for θ: the same tiny-turn recipe with the angle pulled out front.
atoms.visual: n-step slider: (I + ω̂θ/n)ⁿ ghost path with n straight segments approaches the true pink arc as n grows; the gap readout → 0.

atoms.idea: An infinite series is not practical; powers of â satisfy simple formulas that let us sum it in closed form.
atoms.feynman: Instead of climbing infinitely many stairs, notice the stairs repeat in a pattern and take the elevator.
atoms.visual: Show ω̂, ω̂², ω̂³, ω̂⁴ grids in a row; ω̂³ and −ω̂ light up as twins, ω̂⁴ and −ω̂² as twins — the pattern repeats.

atoms.label: Lemma 2.3
atoms.idea: Lemma 2.3: â² = aaᵀ − ‖a‖²I (Eq 2.12) and â³ = −‖a‖²â (Eq 2.13); all higher powers follow recursively.
atoms.feynman: Crossing with a twice kills the part along a and flips the part across it; crossing three times is crossing once, backwards.
atoms.visual: Orange a and teal b: apply â repeatedly and watch b’s across-part rotate 90° each time while its along-part vanishes; after three steps it is −(â b) (coral twin highlight).

atoms.label: Eq (2.14)
atoms.idea: Grouping the odd and even terms yields sin θ and 1 − cos θ series: exp(ω̂θ) = I + ω̂ sin θ + ω̂²(1 − cos θ) — Rodrigues’ formula, an efficient way to compute the rotation.
atoms.feynman: Every point on a turning wheel is “where it was” plus a sideways step of size sin θ plus an inward step of size 1 − cos θ.
atoms.visual: The pink tip’s motion is decomposed into three colored arrows: start position (slate), sin θ·(ω×q) sideways (orange), (1−cos θ)·ω×(ω×q) inward (purple); their tip-to-tail sum lands on the true tip for every θ. Matrix panel: I + sin θ·ω̂ + (1−cos θ)·ω̂² equals the series sum.

atoms.label: Rodrigues, non-unit ω
atoms.idea: If ‖ω‖ ≠ 1, divide out the length: exp(ω̂θ) = I + (ω̂/‖ω‖) sin(‖ω‖θ) + (ω̂²/‖ω‖²)(1 − cos(‖ω‖θ)) (Exercise 12). Next: check that exp(ω̂θ) really is a rotation.
atoms.feynman: Spinning twice as fast for the same time is the same as spinning at normal speed for twice as long.
atoms.visual: Let the orange axis arrow be stretched; the angle readout becomes ‖ω‖θ and the motion matches the unit-axis version with θ scaled.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Proposition 2.4: exp of a skew matrix is in SO(3) (inverse = transpose, det = +1 by continuity). Proposition 2.5: every rotation is such an exponential; the constructive proof begins.

atoms.label: Prop 2.4
atoms.idea: Proposition 2.4: for ω̂ ∈ so(3) and θ ∈ R, exp(ω̂θ) ∈ SO(3).
atoms.feynman: However long you keep spinning a top, it is still the same top, just turned.
atoms.visual: Leave θ and ω free; the RᵀR = I and det = +1 badges stay lime for every setting.

atoms.label: Prop 2.4 step 1
atoms.idea: Step 1: [exp(ω̂θ)]⁻¹ = exp(−ω̂θ) = exp(ω̂ᵀθ) = [exp(ω̂θ)]ᵀ, using skew-symmetry; so R⁻¹ = Rᵀ.
atoms.feynman: Undoing a spin is spinning the other way; and for a skew grid “the other way” is the same as flipping the grid over.
atoms.visual: Staircase tile 1: play exp(ω̂θ) then exp(−ω̂θ) — the body returns home; tile 2: the −ω̂ grid and the transposed ω̂ grid flash identical.

atoms.label: Prop 2.4 step 2
atoms.idea: Step 2: det R = ±1, and det of exp is continuous in θ starting at det exp(0) = 1; it cannot jump to −1, so det R = +1.
atoms.feynman: A light that can only show +1 or −1 and changes smoothly can never switch — it stays at what it started with.
atoms.visual: A det readout plotted against θ as you sweep: a flat lime line at +1; a coral “−1” band is drawn but the line can never reach it without a jump.

atoms.idea: Geometric reading: a skew matrix is an axis (via ω ↦ ω̂), the exponential turns it into rotation by θ about that axis — hence the name so(3). Next: every rotation arises this way (exp is onto).
atoms.feynman: Every arrow is a “spin recipe”; cooking the recipe gives a turned object.
atoms.visual: Arrow-to-pose machine: drop any orange arrow into the funnel, out comes the blue body turned about that arrow by its length.

atoms.label: Prop 2.5
atoms.idea: Proposition 2.5: for every R ∈ SO(3) there is a unit ω and an angle θ with R = exp(ω̂θ).
atoms.feynman: No matter how you’ve turned a toy, there is one single axis and one single swing that would have gotten it there.
atoms.visual: Drop a random gold target orientation; a “find axis” button produces an orange axis and θ, and a single spin carries the start body onto the target (lime overlap).

atoms.label: Prop 2.5 setup
atoms.idea: Constructive proof: write R entrywise (Eq 2.15) and expand Rodrigues in components using v_θ = 1 − cos θ, c_θ, s_θ, then match entries.
atoms.feynman: To find which way a door was swung, compare the door’s numbers with the general recipe’s numbers, slot by slot.
atoms.visual: Two 3×3 grids side by side: the target R (gold numbers) and the Rodrigues template (orange symbols in ω, θ); matching cells pulse in pairs.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Expanded Rodrigues matrix (Eq 2.16). Trace gives θ = arccos((tr R − 1)/2) (Eq 2.17) — valid because eigenvalues have modulus 1; off-diagonal differences give ω (Eq 2.18). The map is many-to-one; ωθ are the exponential coordinates.

atoms.label: Eq (2.16)
atoms.idea: Rodrigues expanded entrywise: diagonal entries ωᵢ²v_θ + c_θ; off-diagonals ωᵢωⱼv_θ ∓ ω_k s_θ.
atoms.feynman: The recipe written out ingredient by ingredient for each of the nine slots.
atoms.visual: The orange template grid fills with formulas; hovering a cell highlights which of ω₁, ω₂, ω₃ (red, green, blue) and which of sin/cos feed it.

atoms.idea: Matching the diagonal: trace(R) = 1 + 2 cos θ.
atoms.feynman: Add up how much each axis still points the way it used to: the more you turned, the smaller the total.
atoms.visual: Three diagonal cells glow and sum into a trace bar; as θ sweeps 0→π the bar drops from 3 to −1 along a 1 + 2cos θ curve.

atoms.label: Eq (2.17)
atoms.idea: Eigenvalues of R have modulus 1 and come in conjugate pairs, so −1 ≤ tr R ≤ 3 and θ = arccos((tr R − 1)/2) exists; θ is only determined up to ±θ + 2πn.
atoms.feynman: The total can never go below −1 or above 3, so there is always an angle that explains it — though turning left 30° or right 330° explains it equally well.
atoms.visual: Eigenvalues plotted as dots on the unit circle (1, e^{±iθ}); their sum is the trace bar; ghost θ and −θ+2π markers show the ambiguity.

atoms.label: Eq (2.18)
atoms.idea: Off-diagonal differences give r₃₂−r₂₃ = 2ω₁s_θ etc.; for θ ≠ 0, ω = (r₃₂−r₂₃, r₁₃−r₃₁, r₂₁−r₁₂)/(2 sin θ).
atoms.feynman: The lopsidedness of the grid (how different it is from its mirror image) points along the spin axis.
atoms.visual: Grid minus its transpose → a skew grid, read back as an orange arrow via vee; divided by 2 sin θ it becomes the unit axis, drawn on the body.

atoms.idea: Choosing 2π − θ gives axis −ω; exp is many-to-one. At R = I, θ = 0 and ω is arbitrary; otherwise there are exactly two (ω, θ) pairs with θ ∈ [0, 2π).
atoms.feynman: Turning 90° clockwise looking down equals turning 270° counter-clockwise; and if you didn’t turn at all, any axis “did” it.
atoms.visual: Two ghost solutions drawn together: (ω, θ) orange and (−ω, 2π−θ) dashed; at R = I the orange axis spins freely with a coral “any” halo.

atoms.label: exponential coordinates
atoms.idea: The vector ωθ ∈ R³ is the exponential coordinates of R; Props 2.4 and 2.5 together give Euler’s theorem.
atoms.feynman: One arrow whose direction is the hinge and whose length is the swing — that single arrow says everything about the turn.
atoms.visual: An orange arrow ωθ inside the radius-π ball; drag it and the body follows; its length is the angle readout.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Euler’s theorem (Thm 2.6): every orientation is one rotation about a fixed axis; the axis–angle form is non-unique and singular at R = I. Other representations: ZYZ Euler angles built from elementary rotations Rx, Ry, Rz.

atoms.label: Thm 2.6
atoms.idea: Theorem 2.6 (Euler): any orientation R equals a rotation about some fixed axis ω by an angle θ ∈ [0, 2π).
atoms.feynman: However a ball has been turned in your hands, there is a skewer through it that you could have twisted it about in one go.
atoms.visual: Random gold target pose → orange skewer appears through the body; a single θ swing about it lands the body on the target. Re-roll many times: it always works (lime counter).

atoms.idea: The equivalent-axis representation is not unique ((−ω, 2π−θ) gives the same R) and has a singularity at R = I, where the axis is arbitrary and stops depending smoothly on R.
atoms.feynman: A weathervane in dead-calm air: when nothing is turning, the arrow could point anywhere and a tiny breeze makes it jump.
atoms.visual: Drag the body toward the identity; the orange axis readout jitters wildly near θ = 0 while θ itself shrinks smoothly to 0 — a coral “axis undefined” halo at the very centre of the ball.

atoms.idea: Subsection 2.2.3 heading: Other representations.
Exponential coordinates are the canonical coordinates of SO(3); other coordinate systems (Euler angles, quaternions, more in the exercises) are related back to them.
atoms.feynman: Many languages can describe the same turn; the exponential is the “native tongue” we translate from.
atoms.visual: A hub icon 🌀 (exp coords) with spokes to 🎛️ (Euler), 🪢 (quaternion), 🧭 (matrix); the same body pose shown with all four readouts at once.

atoms.idea: Heading: Euler angles.
ZYZ Euler angles: starting aligned with A, turn B by α about its z, then by β about its new y, then by γ about its newest z; the triple (α, β, γ) names the orientation.
atoms.feynman: Aiming a desk lamp: swivel the base, tilt the arm, then spin the shade.
atoms.visual: A gimbal of three orange rings holding a blue body; three dials α, β, γ; each dial animates its turn about the body’s CURRENT axis (the axis glyph highlights before it turns).

atoms.label: Rx, Ry, Rz
atoms.idea: The three basic single-axis rotations: R_x(φ) = exp(x̂φ), R_y(β) = exp(ŷβ), R_z(α) = exp(ẑα), each a 3×3 matrix with a cos/sin block in the plane perpendicular to the axis.
atoms.feynman: Spinning a coin about one edge, about another edge, or flat on the table: three basic twists.
atoms.visual: Three mini-panels, each with a single axis (red, green, blue) and a dial; the 3×3 grid shows the unchanged axis row/column in its color and a cos/sin 2×2 block that cycles as the dial turns.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Viewing B as fixed makes all turns about fixed axes; inverting gives R_ab = Rz(α)Ry(β)Rz(γ) (Eq 2.19). Euler angles can be solved from R with atan2 when sin β ≠ 0 (Eq 2.20) but are singular at R = I. ZYX (yaw–pitch–roll) and YZX alternatives exist.

atoms.idea: Trick: treat B as fixed so A turns about fixed axes; then R_ba = Rz(−γ)Ry(−β)Rz(−α).
atoms.feynman: Instead of turning the lamp, keep the lamp still and walk around it the opposite way — the view is the same.
atoms.visual: Camera-lock toggle: lock the camera to B and watch the world frame A swing through −α, −β, −γ about fixed axes.

atoms.label: Eq (2.19)
atoms.idea: Inverting gives R_ab = Rz(α)Ry(β)Rz(γ), written out with cosines and sines of the three angles.
atoms.feynman: Undo the walk-around in reverse order and you get the lamp’s turns in their natural order.
atoms.visual: Three small grids multiply left-to-right into one big grid; each entry of the product is colored by which dials it depends on; dragging any dial updates the product and the body.

atoms.label: Eq (2.20)
atoms.idea: Every such product is a rotation, and conversely every R has ZYZ angles: for sin β ≠ 0, β = atan2(√(r₃₁²+r₃₂²), r₃₃), α = atan2(r₂₃/s_β, r₁₃/s_β), γ = atan2(r₃₂/s_β, −r₃₁/s_β); atan2 uses both signs to pick the quadrant.
atoms.feynman: Given where the lamp shade ended up, you can work out the swivel, tilt and spin — as long as the arm isn’t straight up.
atoms.visual: Inverse mode: trackball-drag the body freely; the three dials move by themselves to match (atan2 readouts); a quadrant wheel shows atan2 choosing the right quarter.

atoms.idea: ZYZ angles are a local parameterisation: at R = I there is no smooth inverse, since every (α, 0, −α) gives the identity — infinitely many representations.
atoms.feynman: When the lamp arm points straight up, swivelling the base and spinning the shade do the same thing — you can’t tell them apart.
atoms.visual: Set β → 0: the first and last rings line up (coral flash), α and γ dials merge into one coral “α+γ” knob; a fan of ghost dial settings (α, 0, −α) all produce the same lime body.

atoms.idea: Other axis orders give other Euler angles: ZYX (Fick; also yaw–pitch–roll, applied roll about body x, pitch about body y, yaw about body z) and YZX (Helmholtz); these avoid the singularity at the identity. (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: An aeroplane: roll the wings, nose up or down, then turn left or right.
atoms.visual: Convention selector ZYZ / ZYX / YZX: the gimbal rebuilds with the new ring order; a ✈️ glyph replaces the body for yaw–pitch–roll.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: ZYX angles are singular at pitch = −π/2; no 3-parameter representation of SO(3) is singularity-free (like charting a sphere). Quaternions: 4-number global representation; definition, i,j,k rules, conjugate, norm, inverse, and the scalar/vector product formula.

atoms.idea: ZYX angles R = exp(ẑψ)exp(ŷθ)exp(x̂φ) are fine at I but singular at θ = −π/2; topologically, every 3-number chart of SO(3) has singularities somewhere, just as no single flat map covers a sphere.
atoms.feynman: Point a plane straight down: now “roll” and “yaw” are the same motion. And every flat map of the Earth tears somewhere.
atoms.visual: ZYX mode: drag pitch to ±90° → rings align, roll and yaw merge (coral). Side panel: try to peel a globe onto a flat sheet — a coral tear always appears; move the tear, never remove it.

atoms.idea: Heading: Quaternions.

Quaternions extend complex numbers; just as unit complex numbers encode planar rotations, unit quaternions encode 3-D rotations, globally and with no singular poses, at the price of one extra number (four rather than three).
atoms.feynman: A clock hand can be described by a point on a circle; a 3-D turn can be described by a point on a “circle one size up”.
atoms.visual: 2D warm-up: a dial on the unit circle e^{iθ} rotating a planar arrow; then a 4-bar meter appears for 3D (slate q0, red q1, green q2, blue q3).

atoms.label: quaternion
atoms.idea: A quaternion Q = q₀ + q₁i + q₂j + q₃k = (q₀, q⃗); quaternions form a 4-D real vector space with an associative, distributive but non-commutative product, with i² = j² = k² = ijk = −1, ij = −ji = k, jk = −kj = i, ki = −ik = j.
atoms.feynman: Three special “turn” buttons i, j, k: pressing i then j is not the same as j then i — just like turning a book about two different edges.
atoms.visual: A multiplication wheel i → j → k: going clockwise gives +, counter-clockwise gives − (coral). Tap two buttons in either order and see the result flip sign.

atoms.label: conjugate
atoms.idea: Conjugate Q* = (q₀, −q⃗); ‖Q‖² = QQ* = q₀² + ‖q⃗‖²; inverse Q⁻¹ = Q*/‖Q‖²; identity (1, 0).
atoms.feynman: The conjugate is the mirror instruction: same amount, opposite direction — doing both cancels out.
atoms.visual: Conjugate button flips the three colored bars; Q·Q* collapses to a single slate bar of height ‖Q‖² with the vector bars at zero.

atoms.label: quaternion product
atoms.idea: Product in vector form: Q·P = (q₀p₀ − q⃗·p⃗, q₀p⃗ + p₀q⃗ + q⃗ × p⃗).
atoms.feynman: Combining two turns: the “how much” part shrinks by how much the axes agree, and the axis part mixes both axes plus a sideways bit.
atoms.visual: Arrows for q⃗ and p⃗; the result’s vector part is drawn as three tip-to-tail arrows q₀p⃗, p₀q⃗, q⃗×p⃗ (the last in coral). Swap P and Q: only the coral arrow reverses.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Unit quaternions form a group; R = exp(ω̂θ) ↦ Q = (cos θ/2, ω sin θ/2); products of quaternions match compositions of rotations; extraction formula back to (ω, θ). Section 2.3 begins: rigid transformations map frames to frames; pure translation tracks one point.

atoms.idea: The vector-form product usually replaces the i, j, k table in practice.
atoms.feynman: Once you know the shortcut, you stop reciting the times tables.
atoms.visual: The i/j/k wheel fades out and the dot/cross formula panel stays.

atoms.label: unit quaternion
atoms.idea: Unit quaternions (‖Q‖ = 1) form a group (Exercise 6); a rotation exp(ω̂θ) is assigned Q = (cos(θ/2), ω sin(θ/2)).
atoms.feynman: A quaternion only uses half the turn — like a ribbon tied to a spinning ball that needs two full turns to untangle.
atoms.visual: Drag θ: the slate bar follows cos(θ/2) and the colored bars follow ω sin(θ/2); a lime ring confirms the squared bars sum to 1. Spin 360°: the body is home but the bars read −Q (coral); spin 720° and Q returns (lime); a ribbon from the body to the wall shows the belt trick.

atoms.label: Q_ac = Q_ab·Q_bc
atoms.idea: Composition: Q_ac = Q_ab · Q_bc mirrors R_ac = R_ab R_bc, so quaternion multiplication is rotation composition.
atoms.feynman: Chaining two turns in quaternion-speak gives the same answer as chaining them as matrices — two languages, same story.
atoms.visual: Two orange trackballs; the body is driven once by R_ab R_bc and once (ghost) by the quaternion product converted back; they coincide (lime).

atoms.label: quaternion → (ω, θ)
atoms.idea: Extraction: θ = 2 arccos q₀, ω = q⃗ / sin(θ/2) if θ ≠ 0 (else 0), then R = exp(ω̂θ).
atoms.feynman: From the half-turn ribbon you can read back the hinge and the full swing.
atoms.visual: Type or drag the 4 bars; the orange axis and θ readout reconstruct and the body snaps to exp(ω̂θ).

atoms.idea: Because the group structures match, quaternions are an efficient, singularity-free rotation representation.
atoms.feynman: Four numbers, never jammed — the globe instead of the torn map.
atoms.visual: Re-run the Euler lock drag in quaternion mode: the 4 bars move smoothly through the pose where the Euler dials jammed (lime trace vs coral spike).

atoms.idea: Section 2.3 heading: Rigid Motion in R³.

Rigid motions keep distances and angles; we describe them by the pose of a body frame relative to an inertial frame, and call any transformation between frames a rigid (body) transformation, body or no body.
atoms.feynman: A pose is just “where is the frame and which way does it face” — whether the frame is glued to a robot hand or is imaginary.
atoms.visual: Slate frame A and a blue frame B floating free (no body drawn); the same 4×4 readout as later appears, showing a frame alone carries the full pose.

atoms.idea: Rigid motion = rotation + translation; translation alone is easy: follow one point of the body. (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: To know how far a car drove, watch just its hood ornament.
atoms.visual: Freeze rotation; drag B; a teal trail behind its origin alone is p(t).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.3; a configuration is (p_ab, R_ab) and the configuration space is SE(3) = R³ × SO(3) (Eq 2.21), generalised to SE(n). An element also transforms coordinates: q_a = p_ab + R_ab q_b (Eq 2.22).

atoms.label: Fig 2.3
atoms.idea: Figure 2.3: inertial frame A, body frame B with origin offset p_ab and orientation, the transform g_ab between them, and a point q on the body.
atoms.feynman: A room and a box in it: an arrow from the room’s corner to the box’s corner, plus the box’s tilt.
atoms.visual: Slate A at the origin, blue B elsewhere, teal arrow p_ab from A’s origin to B’s, pink point q on B.

atoms.idea: Tracking one point’s curve p(t) describes the whole translational trajectory.
atoms.feynman: The hood ornament’s path is the car’s path.
atoms.visual: Teal trail of B’s origin continues as you drag.

atoms.label: Eq (2.21)
atoms.idea: General motion: configuration (p_ab, R_ab) — position of B’s origin and orientation of B in A; the configuration space is SE(3) = R³ × SO(3), the special Euclidean group (group property shown next); SE(n) = Rⁿ × SO(n).
atoms.feynman: A drone’s state is “where” (three numbers) plus “which way it faces” (a turn): two separate dials bolted together.
atoms.visual: Two control widgets: a teal 3-D position handle and an orange trackball; together they place B; readout pair (p, R).

atoms.label: Eq (2.22)
atoms.idea: (p, R) also converts coordinates: q_a = p_ab + R_ab q_b, i.e. g(q) = p + Rq.
atoms.feynman: Directions given relative to the box: first turn them to match the box’s tilt, then add where the box is.
atoms.visual: Pink q: body numbers q_b fixed; animation first rotates the q_b arrow by R (orange), then adds teal p_ab tip-to-tail; endpoint matches q_a readout.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Vectors transform by rotation only. Homogeneous coordinates: points get a trailing 1, vectors a trailing 0, which encodes the point/vector syntax rules; the affine map becomes the linear 4×4 map ḡ = [R p; 0 1] (Eq 2.23).

atoms.label: g* v = Rv
atoms.idea: q_a = g_ab(q_b); a vector v = s − r transforms as g*(v) = g(s) − g(r) = R(s − r) = Rv — translation cancels, vectors only rotate.
atoms.feynman: Moving a room doesn’t change “three steps north” from the bed to the door — unless you turn the room.
atoms.visual: Two arrows on the body: a point arrow from A’s origin (shifts with p) and a free teal vector (only turns). Translate-only drag: the free vector is unchanged (lime).

atoms.idea: Subsection 2.3.1 heading: Homogeneous representation.

atoms.label: homogeneous coords
atoms.idea: Homogeneous coordinates: append 1 to a point (q̄ = (q, 1); origin (0,0,0,1)) and 0 to a vector (v̄ = (v, 0)).
atoms.feynman: Give every point a “here!” flag set to 1 and every arrow a flag set to 0, so you never confuse a place with a direction.
atoms.visual: Every pink point carries a fourth slot showing 1 (gold) and every teal vector a fourth slot showing 0 (slate).

atoms.idea: The 1/0 flag enforces syntax: vector ± vector = vector (0), point + vector = point (1), point − point = vector (0), point + point = meaningless (2).
atoms.feynman: Adding “3 steps north” to “the bed” gives a place; adding the bed to the door gives nonsense.
atoms.visual: Drag-and-drop arithmetic bench: combine tokens; the fourth slot adds up — 0 or 1 glows lime, a 2 glows coral 🚫.

atoms.label: Eq (2.23)
atoms.idea: The affine map q_a = p_ab + R_ab q_b becomes linear in 4-D: q̄_a = ḡ_ab q̄_b with ḡ = [R p; 0 1], the homogeneous representation of g.
atoms.feynman: Folding “turn then shift” into one machine: one multiplication now does both.
atoms.visual: A 4×4 grid: 3×3 rotation block (axis colors), teal p column, slate bottom row 0 0 0 1. Multiply by a point (…,1): the p column is picked up; by a vector (…,0): it is ignored (p column dims).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Cost: dimension 3 → 4; graphics uses the last row for scaling and perspective, which are no longer rigid. Composition is matrix multiplication (Eq 2.24); SE(3) is a group with inverse [Rᵀ −Rᵀp; 0 1]. Vectors transform by ḡ v̄ too.

atoms.idea: The price of a linear representation is going from 3 to 4 dimensions.
atoms.feynman: To carry both a turn and a shift in one box, you need a slightly bigger box.
atoms.visual: A 3-slot vector grows a fourth slot with a little 🪄; the matrix grows a row and column.

atoms.idea: In computer graphics the bottom-right 1 may become a scale factor (dilation/contraction) and the zero row a perspective row; those matrices are no longer rigid.
atoms.feynman: A camera lens can shrink or warp a picture, but a real object never shrinks when you pick it up.
atoms.visual: Unlock the bottom row: drag the corner entry and the body inflates (coral “not rigid” — distance readouts change); drag a bottom-row entry and the body warps into perspective.

atoms.label: Eq (2.24)
atoms.idea: Composition: ḡ_ac = ḡ_ab ḡ_bc = [R_ab R_bc, R_ab p_bc + p_ab; 0 1]; composition is ordinary matrix multiplication, and SE(3) is a group.
atoms.feynman: Directions from the room to the shelf and from the shelf to the book chain into directions from the room to the book.
atoms.visual: Three frames A → B → C with teal offset arrows; C’s position in A is shown as R_ab p_bc (rotated offset, orange) + p_ab, landing on the true origin of C (lime).

atoms.label: SE(3) group
atoms.idea: Group checks: closure of products, identity I₄, inverse ḡ⁻¹ = [Rᵀ −Rᵀp; 0 1] (so g⁻¹ = (−Rᵀp, Rᵀ)), and associativity.
atoms.feynman: To walk back from the shelf to the room: turn back first, then walk the turned-back arrow in reverse.
atoms.visual: Inverse button: an arrow flips from B→A; the scene shows −Rᵀp drawn in B’s axes, and ḡ ḡ⁻¹ collapses to I₄ (lime).

atoms.label: ḡ v̄
atoms.idea: With the 0 in a vector’s last slot, ḡ v̄ = (Rv, 0): matrix multiplication also implements the action on vectors. (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: The same machine moves places and arrows; the flag tells it whether to shift.
atoms.visual: Feed the 4×4 grid a vector token (…,0): the output is the rotated arrow and the translation column stays dim.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.4. Notation: write gq, gv for homogeneous products. Proposition 2.7: every g ∈ SE(3) preserves distances and cross products, inheriting the proofs for rotations. Example 2.1 (rotation about a line) begins.

atoms.label: Fig 2.4
atoms.idea: Figure 2.4: frame B rotates by θ about a vertical line through (0, l₁, 0), offset from frame A.
atoms.feynman: A door on a hinge a step away from where you stand.
atoms.visual: Slate A at origin, an orange vertical hinge line at y = l₁, blue body frame B swinging around it by dial θ.

atoms.idea: Notation: homogeneous and abstract forms are identified; gq and gv mean ḡq̄ and ḡ*v̄.
atoms.feynman: We stop writing the little flags explicitly once everyone knows they are there.
atoms.visual: Toggle that hides the 1/0 slots; the arithmetic still works the same.

atoms.label: Prop 2.7
atoms.idea: Proposition 2.7: any g ∈ SE(3) preserves distances ‖gq − gp‖ = ‖q − p‖ and orientation g*(v × w) = g*v × g*w.
atoms.feynman: Moving and turning a toy never stretches or mirrors it.
atoms.visual: Drag both the teal position handle and the orange trackball; the 📏 and ✋ lights from Definition 2.1 stay lime.

atoms.label: Prop 2.7 proof
atoms.idea: Proof: translations cancel in differences, so both properties reduce to the rotation case (Prop 2.2).
atoms.feynman: Shifting two pebbles together doesn’t change the gap between them; only the turning is left to check, and we already did.
atoms.visual: Staircase: tile 1 — two points shift together, gap readout fixed; tile 2 — replay of the rotation proof.

atoms.label: Ex 2.1
atoms.idea: Example 2.1: rigid body rotated about a z-direction line through (0, l₁, 0) (Fig 2.4); let θ be the rotation amount. (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: A door swinging about its hinge, with the hinge a step to your right.
atoms.visual: Hinge scene from Fig 2.4 with θ dial.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Example 2.1 finished: hinge offset l₁ gives g_ab(θ) = [Rz(θ) (0,l₁,0); 0 1]. Section 2.3.2: the exponential idea extends to SE(3); a revolute link’s tip obeys ṗ = ω × (p − q), which becomes p̄̇ = ξ̂ p̄ with the 4×4 ξ̂ = [ω̂ v; 0 0], v = −ω × q.

atoms.label: Ex 2.1
atoms.idea: Example 2.1 (cont.): orientation R_ab = Rz(θ) and origin p_ab = (0, l₁, 0).
atoms.feynman: The door turns by θ and its corner sits a fixed step from the hinge.
atoms.visual: Hinge scene: the 3×3 block fills with the cos/sin z-rotation pattern as θ turns; the teal p column stays (0, l₁, 0).

atoms.label: g_ab(θ)
atoms.idea: Homogeneous form g_ab(θ) = [Rz(θ), (0, l₁, 0); 0, 1].
atoms.feynman: One card that says both how the door is turned and where its corner is.
atoms.visual: The full 4×4 grid assembled; drag θ and only the rotation block changes.

atoms.idea: At θ = 0 the two frames differ only by a sideways shift along y.
atoms.feynman: Before the door swings, the only difference between you and the door is a step sideways.
atoms.visual: Set θ = 0: the rotation block turns into the identity (lime) and only the teal translation arrow remains.

atoms.idea: Subsection 2.3.2 heading: Exponential coordinates for rigid motion and twists.
The exponential map generalises from SO(3) to SE(3), giving an elegant, geometric description of spatial rigid motion; motivating examples first, then definitions.
atoms.feynman: We already know “spin a tiny bit, many times” gives a rotation; now we spin AND slide a tiny bit, many times.
atoms.visual: Bridge tile: the 🌀 spin-scene thumbnail morphs into a 🔩 helix thumbnail.

atoms.label: Eq (2.25)
atoms.idea: One-link robot rotating at unit rate about unit axis ω through point q: tip velocity ṗ = ω × (p − q).
atoms.feynman: A door’s handle moves around the hinge, not around the middle of the room.
atoms.visual: Orange revolute joint at q with axis ω (drag q around); blue link with pink tip p; pink velocity arrow = ω × (p − q), a lime right-angle mark to the radius from q.

atoms.label: Eq (2.26)
atoms.idea: In homogeneous coordinates this is linear: p̄̇ = ξ̂ p̄ with ξ̂ = [ω̂ v; 0 0] and v = −ω × q.
atoms.feynman: Fold “where the hinge is” into the instructions, and the motion becomes one simple multiply-by-a-matrix rule again.
atoms.visual: 4×4 grid ξ̂: orange ω̂ block, teal v column (drawn as −ω×q from the hinge point), slate zero row. Multiplying by (p, 1) reproduces the pink velocity arrow exactly.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.5 (revolute and prismatic joints). The ODE solves as p̄(t) = exp(ξ̂t) p̄(0); a prismatic joint ṗ = v gives ξ̂ = [0 v; 0 0] (Eq 2.28). These generalise so(3) to se(3) (Eq 2.29).

atoms.label: Fig 2.5
atoms.idea: Figure 2.5: (a) a revolute joint (rotation about axis ω through q) and (b) a prismatic joint (sliding along v).
atoms.feynman: A door hinge and a drawer runner.
atoms.visual: Two side-by-side toy joints: orange hinge with axis ω through q, orange slider rail along v; each carries a blue link with a pink tip p(t).

atoms.label: exp(ξ̂t)
atoms.idea: Solution p̄(t) = exp(ξ̂t) p̄(0), with the usual matrix-exponential series; for unit speed, t is the rotation angle and exp(ξ̂t) maps a point’s start to its location after turning t radians.
atoms.feynman: Swing the door at a steady pace; the stopwatch reading is how far it swung.
atoms.visual: θ slider on the hinge: n tiny straight steps (I + ξ̂θ/n)ⁿ draw a ghost polyline that converges to the pink circular arc around the hinge (gap readout → 0).

atoms.label: Eq (2.27)–(2.28)
atoms.idea: Prismatic joint at unit speed: ṗ = v, so p̄(t) = exp(ξ̂t) p̄(0) with ξ̂ = [0 v; 0 0]; t is the distance slid.
atoms.feynman: A drawer slides straight: every point moves the same way at the same speed.
atoms.visual: Slider joint: every point on the blue link gets an identical teal velocity arrow v; the ξ̂ grid shows an empty rotation block and only the teal v column.

atoms.label: Eq (2.29)
atoms.idea: These 4×4 ξ̂ generalise ω̂ ∈ so(3): se(3) = {(v, ω̂) : v ∈ R³, ω̂ ∈ so(3)}, written ξ̂ = [ω̂ v; 0 0].
atoms.feynman: Every way of “moving a little bit” — turning, sliding, or both — fits on one six-number recipe card.
atoms.visual: The ξ̂ grid with both blocks live: orange ω controls and teal v controls; any combination gives a valid generator (lime).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Elements of se(3) are twists; vee/wedge convert ξ̂ ↔ ξ = (v, ω) ∈ R⁶ (Eqs 2.30–2.31). Proposition 2.8: exp(ξ̂θ) ∈ SE(3); proof case ω = 0 gives [I vθ; 0 1] (Eq 2.32); case ω ≠ 0 conjugates by g = [I ω×v; 0 1] to strip the off-axis part (Eqs 2.33–2.34).

atoms.label: Eq (2.30)–(2.31)
atoms.idea: Members of se(3) are called twists — the infinitesimal generators of rigid motion; ∨ extracts its twist coordinates ξ = (v, ω) ∈ R⁶ and ∧ builds the matrix back, mirroring hat/vee for so(3).
atoms.feynman: A twist is a six-knob mixing desk: three knobs for sliding, three for spinning.
atoms.visual: A 6-bar meter ξ (three teal v bars, three orange ω bars) wired both ways to the 4×4 ξ̂ grid: drag a bar, the grid cell moves; edit the grid, the bar moves.

atoms.label: Prop 2.8
atoms.idea: Proposition 2.8: for any twist ξ̂ and θ ∈ R, exp(ξ̂θ) ∈ SE(3).
atoms.feynman: Follow any steady spin-and-slide recipe for any time and you still have the same unbroken toy, just moved.
atoms.visual: Randomise the 6 bars and θ; the body flows along and the rigid checks (📏, ✋, bottom row 0 0 0 1) stay lime.

atoms.label: Prop 2.8 proof
atoms.idea: Proof by explicit calculation, which also yields a formula for exp(ξ̂θ); split on whether ω = 0.
atoms.feynman: Two kinds of recipe to check: pure sliding, and sliding-with-spinning.
atoms.visual: Staircase header with two doors: “ω = 0” (teal) and “ω ≠ 0” (orange).

atoms.label: Eq (2.32)
atoms.idea: Case ω = 0: ξ̂² = 0, so the series stops: exp(ξ̂θ) = [I vθ; 0 1], a pure translation.
atoms.feynman: Sliding a drawer twice as long moves it twice as far — no curving, nothing extra.
atoms.visual: Staircase tile 1: the ξ̂² grid is all zeros (dim slate); the series bar has only I and ξ̂θ; the body slides straight by vθ.

atoms.label: Eq (2.33)–(2.34)
atoms.idea: Case ω ≠ 0 (scale so ‖ω‖ = 1): conjugate by g = [I ω×v; 0 1]; then ξ̂′ = g⁻¹ξ̂g = [ω̂ hω; 0 0] with h = ωᵀv — the twist seen from a point on its own axis has only along-axis sliding.
atoms.feynman: Stand on the hinge line itself: from there the motion is just spinning plus sliding along the line, no swinging around.
atoms.visual: Staircase tile 2: shift the viewpoint origin (slate) onto the screw axis by the teal arrow ω×v; the teal v column shrinks to an arrow parallel to the orange ω (length h).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Using exp(gΛg⁻¹) = g exp(Λ) g⁻¹ (Eq 2.35) and easy powers of ξ̂′, the closed form exp(ξ̂θ) = [exp(ω̂θ), (I − exp(ω̂θ))(ω×v) + ωωᵀvθ; 0 1] (Eq 2.36). exp(ξ̂θ) maps points from initial to final positions in one frame; g_ab(θ) = exp(ξ̂θ)g_ab(0) (Eq 2.37). Proposition 2.9 (surjectivity) stated.

atoms.label: Eq (2.35)
atoms.idea: Since exp(gΛg⁻¹) = g exp(Λ) g⁻¹ (Exercise 8), compute exp(ξ̂′θ): powers of ξ̂′ just repeat ω̂ⁿ (because ω̂ω = 0), giving exp(ξ̂′θ) = [exp(ω̂θ) hωθ; 0 1].
atoms.feynman: Easier to describe a corkscrew while standing on its axis; then walk back to where you were.
atoms.visual: Staircase tile 3: ξ̂′ powers drawn as grids — the column hω vanishes after the first power; the body spins about the axis while sliding hθ along it.

atoms.label: Eq (2.36)
atoms.idea: Conjugating back: exp(ξ̂θ) = [exp(ω̂θ), (I − exp(ω̂θ))(ω × v) + ωωᵀvθ; 0 1], an element of SE(3).
atoms.feynman: The final answer: turn like the hinge says, and shift by “how far the axis point swung” plus “how far you slid along the axis”.
atoms.visual: Staircase tile 4: the translation column is built from two colored arrows — orange (I − e^{ω̂θ})(ω×v) (swing about an offset axis) and teal ωωᵀvθ (slide along it); their sum lands the body exactly where the n-step flow ends.

atoms.label: Eq (2.37)
atoms.idea: Unlike frame-to-frame maps, exp(ξ̂θ) moves points: p(θ) = exp(ξ̂θ)p(0) with both in one reference frame; for a body, g_ab(θ) = exp(ξ̂θ) g_ab(0) — the exponential is a relative motion.
atoms.feynman: Not “translate my words into your language” but “here is where the cup went after I moved it”.
atoms.visual: A ghost blue body at g_ab(0) and the solid body at g_ab(θ); every pink point has a thin trail along the twist flow, all measured against the one slate frame A.

atoms.idea: To use the exponential as a representation we need every rigid transformation to be an exponential of some twist; a constructive procedure follows.
atoms.feynman: If every move can be undone into a recipe, the recipe card is a complete language for moves.
atoms.visual: Gold target-pose marker appears with a 🔎 “find twist” button (enabled next atom).

atoms.label: Prop 2.9
atoms.idea: Proposition 2.9: every g ∈ SE(3) equals exp(ξ̂θ) for some twist ξ̂ and θ.
atoms.feynman: Wherever you put the cup, one steady spin-and-slide could have taken it there.
atoms.visual: Drop a random gold target; 🔎 computes a twist; an orange axis appears and flowing along it lands the body on the target (lime overlap). Re-roll: always works.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Proof of Prop 2.9: R = I gives a pure translation twist; otherwise solve the rotation for (ω, θ) and then the linear system A v = p (Eq 2.38), where A = (I − exp(ω̂θ))ω̂ + ωωᵀθ is invertible. ξθ are the exponential coordinates of g (many-to-one). Example 2.2 begins.

atoms.label: Prop 2.9 case 1
atoms.idea: Proof, trivial case (I, 0) → θ = 0. Case R = I: take ξ̂ = [0 p/‖p‖; 0 0] and θ = ‖p‖; Eq (2.32) confirms exp(ξ̂θ) = (I, p).
atoms.feynman: If the cup didn’t turn, the recipe is just “slide straight there”.
atoms.visual: Target with no rotation: the orange axis disappears and a teal straight arrow carries the body; θ readout = distance.

atoms.label: Eq (2.38)
atoms.idea: Case R ≠ I: equate exp(ξ̂θ) with g; (ω, θ) come from the rotation part (Prop 2.5), leaving (I − exp(ω̂θ))(ω × v) + ωωᵀvθ = p to solve for v.
atoms.feynman: First figure out the hinge direction and the swing from how the cup is turned; then work out where the hinge line must be to explain where the cup ended up.
atoms.visual: Staircase: tile 1 freezes the orange axis direction and θ from the rotation; tile 2 shows the unknown teal v as a draggable ghost, with the predicted end pose sliding until it matches the gold target.

atoms.label: A invertible
atoms.idea: Solvable because A = (I − exp(ω̂θ))ω̂ + ωωᵀθ is nonsingular for θ ∈ (0, 2π): its two pieces act on orthogonal subspaces (across the axis and along it), so Av = 0 only if v = 0 (Exercise 9).
atoms.feynman: One part of the machine handles sideways moves, the other handles along-the-axis moves; neither can cancel the other, so nothing gets lost.
atoms.visual: Split v into an along-axis teal arrow and an across-axis teal arrow; show A maps the first only along the axis (scaled by θ) and the second only across (a turn-and-shrink); a determinant readout stays non-zero (lime) for θ ∈ (0, 2π).

atoms.label: exp coords of g
atoms.idea: Hence ξθ ∈ R⁶ are the exponential coordinates of g; several twists can exponentiate to the same g (rotation part not unique), which is rarely a problem since usually the twist is given.
atoms.feynman: Like before, many recipes give the same final cup position — but usually someone hands you the recipe, not the cup.
atoms.visual: Ghost alternative twists (ω, θ) vs (−ω, 2π−θ) produce the same gold end pose along different helices.

atoms.label: Ex 2.2
atoms.idea: Example 2.2: rotation about a fixed axis offset in space (Fig 2.6); g_ab has a z-rotation by α and translation (−l₂ sin α, l₁ + l₂ cos α, 0); find its twist coordinates.
atoms.feynman: A swinging arm on a post: where does the far corner go, and which single twist explains it?
atoms.visual: Fig 2.6 scene: slate frame A, vertical orange post at (0, l₁), blue arm of length l₂ ending in frame B; dial α.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.6 and Example 2.2 worked: ω = ẑ, θ = α, then solving A v = p_ab gives a messy v; the resulting twist coordinates of the absolute transform.

atoms.label: Fig 2.6
atoms.idea: Figure 2.6: frame B on an arm of length l₂ rotating by α about a vertical axis at distance l₁ from A.
atoms.feynman: A carousel horse on a pole: the pole is the axis, the horse is frame B.
atoms.visual: Fig 2.6 scene rendered with dial α.

atoms.label: Ex 2.2
atoms.idea: Following Prop 2.9: ω = (0,0,1), θ = α; v must solve [(I − exp(ω̂θ))ω̂ + ωωᵀθ] v = p_ab.
atoms.feynman: The turning part is easy — it’s a carousel spinning about vertical; the hard part is where the axis line is.
atoms.visual: The orange axis direction locks vertical; a 3×3 A grid and the teal p_ab column appear as “A · v = p”.

atoms.label: Ex 2.2 solve
atoms.idea: Expanding A for θ = α and inverting gives v in terms of l₁, l₂ and α — with a 1/(1 − cos α) factor.
atoms.feynman: Solving a little 3-by-3 puzzle gives the answer — but it comes out lumpy.
atoms.visual: Solve animation: v appears as a teal arrow whose length depends on α; sweeping α shows it blowing up as α → 0 (coral).

atoms.label: Ex 2.2 result
atoms.idea: Twist coordinates of g_ab: v = ((l₁ − l₂)/2, (l₁ + l₂) sin α / (2(1 − cos α)), 0), ω = (0,0,1), θ = α.
atoms.feynman: The recipe for jumping straight from the room’s corner to the horse’s pose is clumsy, because the starting pose already had an offset baked in.
atoms.visual: 6-bar readout fills with the α-dependent numbers; the orange axis found by the log sits somewhere odd (not the real post), drawn dashed coral.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.7 (general screw, pure translation). Example 2.2 explained: the relative motion g_ab(α)g_ab(0)⁻¹ has the clean twist (l₁,0,0,0,0,1). Section 2.3.3: screw motion = rotate θ about an axis then translate d along it; pitch h = d/θ.

atoms.label: Fig 2.7
atoms.idea: Figure 2.7: (a) a general screw — point p rotates θ about an axis through q and advances d along it; (b) a pure translation along v by θ.
atoms.feynman: A bolt being screwed into a nut, and a drawer sliding out.
atoms.visual: Two panels: (a) gold axis line through q with pink point p spiralling (rotate θ, advance d); (b) a teal arrow v carrying p to p + θv.

atoms.label: Ex 2.2 relative
atoms.idea: The messy twist came from logging the absolute transform. The relative motion g(α) = g_ab(α)g_ab(0)⁻¹ has the clean twist ξ = (l₁, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1) — pure rotation about the true post.
atoms.feynman: Measure the horse’s ride from where it started, not from the room’s corner, and the recipe is simply “spin about the pole”.
atoms.visual: Toggle absolute/relative: the dashed coral axis jumps onto the real orange post (lime) and the 6-bar meter cleans up to v = (l₁,0,0), ω = (0,0,1).

atoms.idea: Subsection 2.3.3 heading: Screws: a geometric description of twists.
Geometric attributes of a twist: define screw motions and show each twist is naturally tied to a screw.
atoms.feynman: Every recipe card has a picture on the back: a bolt with a certain thread.
atoms.visual: A 6-bar ξ card flips over to reveal a gold bolt drawing.

atoms.label: pitch
atoms.idea: Screw motion: rotate θ about an axis, then translate d along the same axis; pitch h = d/θ, so the advance after θ is hθ.
atoms.feynman: A bolt: each full turn moves it forward by one thread spacing — that spacing per turn is the pitch.
atoms.visual: Blue bolt body on the gold axis; sliders θ (orange) and h; the body spins θ and advances hθ, leaving a pink helix whose coil spacing visibly equals 2πh.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.8 (screw acting on a point). Axis as a directed line l = {q + λω} (Eq 2.39); pure translation has infinite pitch with axis through the origin along v. Definition 2.2: a screw is axis l, pitch h, magnitude M. A point moves to q + exp(ω̂θ)(p − q) + hθω.

atoms.label: Fig 2.8
atoms.idea: Figure 2.8: point p is rotated about the axis through q to q + exp(ω̂θ)(p − q), then advanced along ω by hθ.
atoms.feynman: Swing the handle around the hinge, then lift it along the hinge line.
atoms.visual: Pink point p; a purple arm p − q from the gold axis; first an orange arc to q + e^{ω̂θ}(p−q), then a teal lift hθω.

atoms.label: Eq (2.39)
atoms.idea: The axis is an oriented line, fixed by one of its points q and a unit direction ω: l = {q + λω : λ ∈ R}; valid when rotation is non-zero.
atoms.feynman: A skewer: a spot it goes through and the way it points.
atoms.visual: Gold axis line with a draggable point q and a draggable direction ω; λ ticks along it.

atoms.idea: With zero rotation the axis is the line through the origin along unit v; the pitch is taken to be ∞ and the magnitude is how far it slides.
atoms.feynman: A drawer has no hinge to spin about — call its “thread” infinitely long.
atoms.visual: Set rotation to zero: the gold axis jumps to pass through the origin along v; the pitch readout shows ∞; the body only slides.

atoms.label: Def 2.2
