atoms.idea: Definition 2.2: a screw S = (axis l, pitch h, magnitude M); its motion rotates θ = M about l then translates hθ along l; if h = ∞ it is a pure translation by M along l.
atoms.feynman: Three things describe any bolt move: which bolt (axis), how coarse the thread (pitch), and how much you turn (magnitude).
atoms.visual: Three controls only — axis (gold line handle), pitch slider h (with an ∞ notch), magnitude slider M — fully drive the blue body.

atoms.label: g p
atoms.idea: Effect on a point: g p = q + exp(ω̂θ)(p − q) + hθω; homogeneously g = [exp(ω̂θ), (I − exp(ω̂θ))q + hθω; 0 1].
atoms.feynman: Move to the hinge, swing, move back, then lift — all folded into one card.
atoms.visual: The three-arrow construction from Fig 2.8 is replayed for every teal dot of the body at once; the 4×4 grid assembles from the arrows’ colors.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Screw motion g (Eq 2.40) maps body points from initial to final positions; it equals exp(ξ̂θ) with ξ = (−ω × q + hω, ω); pure translation gives [I θv; 0 1] (Eq 2.41). Conversely each twist has screw coordinates: pitch h = ωᵀv/‖ω‖² (Eq 2.42) and axis through ω×v/‖ω‖² along ω (Eq 2.43).

atoms.label: Eq (2.40)
atoms.idea: Holding for every p, the screw motion is g = [exp(ω̂θ), (I − exp(ω̂θ))q + hθω; 0 1], mapping body points’ initial to final coordinates in the fixed frame.
atoms.feynman: One card that moves every crumb of the bolt correctly at once.
atoms.visual: All body dots move by the same 4×4 grid; trails are helices around the gold axis.

atoms.label: screw → twist
atoms.idea: Matching Eq (2.40) with Eq (2.36): the twist ξ = (v, ω) with v = −ω × q + hω generates this screw (‖ω‖ = 1, θ ≠ 0); a pure rotation (h = 0) has ξ = (−ω × q, ω).
atoms.feynman: Read a bolt’s description and you can write the six-knob recipe card that produces it.
atoms.visual: Move q, ω, h on the screw; the 6-bar ξ meter updates (teal v = −ω×q in orange-ish plus hω along the axis); flowing exp(ξ̂θ) overlays exactly on the screw motion (lime).

atoms.label: Eq (2.41)
atoms.idea: Pure translation: with θ the distance, g = [I θv; 0 1] = exp(ξ̂θ) for ξ = (v, 0). So a screw motion is just flowing along one fixed twist for an amount equal to the screw’s magnitude.
atoms.feynman: A drawer screw is just “slide” on the recipe card.
atoms.visual: Pitch to ∞: the orange ω bars drop to zero, the teal v bars carry everything, the body slides along the gold axis.

atoms.idea: Conversely, every twist ξ = (v, ω) (ω not necessarily unit, possibly zero) defines a screw through its screw coordinates.
atoms.feynman: Every recipe card, however strange, secretly describes some bolt.
atoms.visual: Twist mode: drag any of the 6 bars freely; the gold axis, pitch and magnitude redraw live.

atoms.label: Eq (2.42)
atoms.idea: Pitch h = ωᵀv/‖ω‖²: sliding per unit of turning; infinite when ω = 0.
atoms.feynman: How far the bolt advances per radian: how much of the sliding is lined up with the spinning.
atoms.visual: Split teal v into the part along ω (lime) and across ω (slate); the along-part length over ‖ω‖ is the pitch readout; when ω → 0, h → ∞ (∞ badge).

atoms.label: Eq (2.43)
atoms.idea: Axis: for ω ≠ 0 the line along ω through the point ω × v/‖ω‖²; for ω = 0 the line along v through the origin.
atoms.feynman: The bolt’s centre line is found by asking which line of points only slides and never swings.
atoms.visual: Gold axis line drawn through the point ω×v/‖ω‖² (gold dot); points on it show velocity arrows parallel to the axis while off-axis points swirl around it.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Magnitude M = ‖ω‖ (or ‖v‖ if ω = 0) (Eq 2.44). Proposition 2.10: every screw is generated by a unit twist scaled by M, by construction in the infinite and finite pitch cases. Zero-pitch screws model revolute joints; infinite-pitch screws model prismatic joints.

atoms.label: Eq (2.44)
atoms.idea: Magnitude M = ‖ω‖ if ω ≠ 0, else ‖v‖: net rotation, or net translation for pure slides; with unit ω (or unit v) the twist ξ̂θ has magnitude θ.
atoms.feynman: How much you turned the bolt — or, for a drawer, how far you pulled.
atoms.visual: Magnitude bar = length of the orange ω arrow (or teal v when ω = 0); with unit arrows it equals the θ slider.

atoms.idea: Going the other way: given a screw, build a twist with matching attributes — any such twist yields the screw motion.
atoms.feynman: Given a bolt, write its recipe card.
atoms.visual: Screw mode: drag axis/pitch/magnitude; the 6 bars follow.

atoms.label: Prop 2.10
atoms.idea: Proposition 2.10: for a screw (l, h, M) there is a unit twist ξ whose scaled version Mξ generates the screw motion.
atoms.feynman: Every bolt move is “follow this unit-strength recipe for M seconds”.
atoms.visual: Unit twist ξ drawn as a fixed card; the M slider is the stopwatch; the body follows the screw exactly.

atoms.label: Prop 2.10 case h = ∞
atoms.idea: Proof by construction, θ = M, q on the axis. Infinite pitch: axis l = {q + λv}, ξ̂ = [0 v; 0 0], and exp(ξ̂θ) translates by θ along the axis.
atoms.feynman: For a drawer, the card just says “slide this way”.
atoms.visual: Staircase tile 1: ω bars zero, v unit along the gold axis; the body slides M.

atoms.label: Prop 2.10 case h finite
atoms.idea: Finite pitch: axis l = {q + λω}, ξ̂ = [ω̂, −ω × q + hω; 0 0]; direct calculation shows exp(ξ̂θ) is the screw motion.
atoms.feynman: For a bolt, the card says “spin about here, and creep forward this much per turn”.
atoms.visual: Staircase tile 2: build v from the two pieces (−ω × q in teal, hω in lime along the axis); exp flow overlays the screw motion (lime match).

atoms.idea: Special cases: zero-pitch screws are pure rotations and model revolute joints (axis = joint axis); infinite-pitch screws are pure translations and model prismatic joints, with axis along the translation direction through the origin. (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: A door hinge is a bolt with no thread; a drawer is a bolt with an infinitely long thread.
atoms.visual: Pitch slider with snap points at 0 (an orange hinge icon 🚪 appears) and ∞ (a slider-rail icon appears); robot joint glyphs appear next to each.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Unit twists (magnitude 1) let joint motions be written exp(ξ̂θ). The screw formula is independent of which axis point q is used, and axis points move purely by hθ. Chasles’ theorem (Thm 2.11). Exponentials are relative motions: g_ab(θ) = exp(ξ̂θ)g_ab(0) (Eq 2.45). Example 2.3 begins.

atoms.idea: Any line parallel to the translation could serve as the axis of a pure translation; the magnitude is the displacement.
atoms.feynman: For a drawer it doesn’t matter which rail you call “the” rail; they all point the same way.
atoms.visual: In ∞-pitch mode, drag the gold axis sideways: the motion is unchanged (lime).

atoms.label: unit twist
atoms.idea: A unit twist has ‖ω‖ = 1, or ω = 0 and ‖v‖ = 1 (magnitude 1); then revolute and prismatic joint motions are g = exp(ξ̂θ) with θ the joint angle or travel.
atoms.feynman: Calibrate each joint so “1 on the dial” means one radian or one metre.
atoms.visual: A unit-twist badge lights when the 6-bar card is normalised; the joint dial θ then directly reads radians or metres.

atoms.idea: The screw formula doesn’t depend on which point q on the axis is chosen (q′ = q + λω gives the same g), and points on the axis just translate by hθ.
atoms.feynman: A skewer can be grabbed anywhere along its length; and the skewer itself only slides, it never swings.
atoms.visual: Drag q along the gold axis: the 4×4 grid stays frozen (lime). Teal dots placed on the axis move straight along it by hθ while off-axis dots spiral.

atoms.label: Thm 2.11
atoms.idea: Theorem 2.11 (Chasles): any rigid displacement can be achieved by turning about one line while sliding along that same line; this drops straight out of the screw attributes of a twist.
atoms.feynman: Any way you move a book from desk to shelf, there is one bolt you could have screwed it along instead.
atoms.visual: Chasles mode: drop two random poses (ghost start, gold goal); the scene logs the relative transform, draws the screw axis, and plays one helix that joins them. Re-roll ten times: ten lime successes.
atoms.beat: 🎯 Chasles: every move is a screw

atoms.label: Eq (2.45)
atoms.idea: exp(ξ̂θ) is a relative motion in one frame: p(θ) = exp(ξ̂θ)p(0); a frame B riding the screw has g_ab(θ) = exp(ξ̂θ)g_ab(0): first map B-coordinates to A, then move the point within A.
atoms.feynman: First say where the cup is in the room, then say how it was moved within the room.
atoms.visual: Two-step animation for a pink point: g_ab(0) carries its B-numbers into A (dashed arrow), then the helix flow moves it to the final spot (solid arrow); the product grid matches the live frame.
atoms.beat: 🎯 Chasles: every move is a screw

atoms.label: Ex 2.3
atoms.idea: Example 2.3: a body rotating about a fixed vertical axis is a zero-pitch screw along ω = (0,0,1) through q = (0, l₁, 0). (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: The swinging door again, now described as a thread-less bolt.
atoms.visual: Fig 2.9 scene: hinge line at (0, l₁), pitch locked to 0.
atoms.beat: 🎯 Chasles: every move is a screw

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.9 and Example 2.3: twist ξ = (l₁, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1); its exponential rotates points about the line; composing with g_ab(0) = [I (0,l₁,0); 0 1] recovers the configuration found in Example 2.1.

atoms.label: Fig 2.9
atoms.idea: Figure 2.9: frame B rotating by θ about a vertical axis through q = (0, l₁, 0), viewed from frame A.
atoms.feynman: A door on a hinge a step away.
atoms.visual: Hinge scene with orange axis line ω through q, blue frame B, dial θ.
atoms.beat: 🎯 Chasles: every move is a screw

atoms.label: Ex 2.3 twist
atoms.idea: The twist is ξ = (−ω × q, ω) = (l₁, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1).
atoms.feynman: The recipe: spin about vertical; the sideways number l₁ is the hinge’s offset in disguise.
atoms.visual: The teal −ω×q arrow drawn at the origin points along +x with length l₁; the 6-bar card shows (l₁,0,0 | 0,0,1).

atoms.label: Ex 2.3 exp
atoms.idea: exp(ξ̂θ) = [Rz(θ), (l₁ sin θ, l₁(1 − cos θ), 0); 0 1]; applied to a point it moves it, in A coordinates, to where it lands after turning θ about the line.
atoms.feynman: The card tells each crumb of the door where to go after a swing of θ.
atoms.visual: The translation column’s two non-zero entries are drawn as a teal arrow that traces a circle of radius l₁ as θ sweeps — the origin of A swinging around the hinge.

atoms.label: Ex 2.3 config
atoms.idea: The configuration is g_ab(θ) = exp(ξ̂θ) g_ab(0) with g_ab(0) = translation by (0, l₁, 0); multiplying gives [Rz(θ), (0, l₁, 0); 0 1], matching Example 2.1.
atoms.feynman: Start pose times the swing equals what we got by just looking at the door earlier — two routes, same answer.
atoms.visual: Grid product exp(ξ̂θ)·g_ab(0) computed live next to the Example 2.1 grid; cells match (lime) at every θ.
atoms.beat: 🎯 Chasles: every move is a screw

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Section 2.4: velocity on SE(3) needs care because ġ is neither in SE(3) nor se(3); twists are the right representation. 2.4.1: for R_ab(t), a body point’s spatial velocity is Ṙ_ab q_b (Eq 2.46) — nine numbers; rewriting via ṘR⁻¹ (Eq 2.47), Lemma 2.12 says ṘR⁻¹ and R⁻¹Ṙ are skew.

atoms.idea: Section 2.4 heading: Velocity of a Rigid Body.

For a particle, velocity is just dq/dt; for a rigid motion g(t) ∈ SE(3) this naive idea fails since SE(3) is not a vector space — ġ lies in neither SE(3) nor se(3) — so we must relate it carefully to rotational and translational velocity; twists turn out to be the right tool.
atoms.feynman: A bead on a wire has one speed; a tumbling box has every crumb moving differently — you need a smarter summary than “the speed”.
atoms.visual: A tumbling blue box with dozens of pink velocity arrows all different; a raw ġ 4×4 grid beside it is marked with a coral “not a pose, not a twist” badge — until it is multiplied by g⁻¹ (next beats).

atoms.idea: Subsection 2.4.1 heading: Rotational velocity.

atoms.label: spatial / body frame
atoms.idea: Pure rotation: body frame B shares A’s origin and rotates as R_ab(t); A is the spatial frame, B the body frame; a body point has fixed q_b and spatial path q_a(t) = R_ab(t) q_b.
atoms.feynman: A sticker on a spinning globe: its address on the globe never changes, but its position in the room does.
atoms.visual: Slate frame A, blue frame B co-located and spinning; a pink sticker q shows constant body numbers (blue panel) and changing world numbers (slate panel).

atoms.label: Eq (2.46)
atoms.idea: Spatial velocity of the point: v_qa = d/dt q_a = Ṙ_ab q_b.
atoms.feynman: How fast the sticker moves through the room depends on how fast the globe’s orientation is changing.
atoms.visual: Pink velocity arrow on the sticker computed as Ṙ q_b (finite difference of the trackball pose).

atoms.label: Eq (2.47)
atoms.idea: Ṙ needs nine numbers — wasteful; rewrite v_qa = (Ṙ_ab R_ab⁻¹)(R_ab q_b), and the bracketed matrix will be skew.
atoms.feynman: Nine dials to describe a spin is like using nine words where three will do.
atoms.visual: The 9 cells of Ṙ flicker (coral “9”); multiplying by R⁻¹ condenses it into a grid with zero diagonal and mirrored ± cells — only 3 distinct numbers (lime “3”).

atoms.label: Lemma 2.12
atoms.idea: Lemma 2.12: for a curve R(t) in SO(3), both ṘR⁻¹ and R⁻¹Ṙ are skew-symmetric.
atoms.feynman: However a ball is spinning at this instant, its spin can be described by one arrow.
atoms.visual: Both grids (ṘRᵀ in slate, RᵀṘ in blue) are always skew while you swirl the trackball — mirror-cell checks stay lime.

atoms.idea: Footnote: here “spatial” means relative to a fixed inertial frame, not “3-D as opposed to planar”.
atoms.feynman: “Spatial” here means “as the room sees it”.
atoms.visual: The slate world frame gets a small 🌍 tag used consistently for every “spatial” readout.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Proof of Lemma 2.12 by differentiating RRᵀ = I. Spatial angular velocity ω̂ˢ = ṘR⁻¹ (Eq 2.48), body angular velocity ω̂ᵇ = R⁻¹Ṙ (Eq 2.49), related by ωᵇ = R⁻¹ωˢ (Eq 2.50). Point velocities: v_qa = ωˢ × q_a (Eq 2.51), v_qb = ωᵇ × q_b (Eq 2.52).

atoms.label: Lemma 2.12 proof
atoms.idea: Differentiate RRᵀ = I: ṘRᵀ + RṘᵀ = 0, so ṘRᵀ = −(ṘRᵀ)ᵀ — skew; likewise from RᵀR = I for RᵀṘ.
atoms.feynman: If the columns must stay unit and square to each other, any change must be a pure swirl — stretching is forbidden.
atoms.visual: Staircase: tile 1 shows RRᵀ = I as a frozen lime identity grid; tile 2 its time-derivative ṘRᵀ + (ṘRᵀ)ᵀ = 0 as cancelling cell pairs (lime against coral).

atoms.label: Eq (2.48)
atoms.idea: Spatial angular velocity ωˢ_ab ∈ R³ defined by ω̂ˢ = Ṙ_ab R_ab⁻¹: the spin as seen from the fixed frame A.
atoms.feynman: The spin arrow of a merry-go-round, as described by someone standing on the ground.
atoms.visual: Orange arrow ωˢ drawn in slate world axes with 🌍 tag; its three numbers are the vee of the slate skew grid.

atoms.label: Eq (2.49)
atoms.idea: Body angular velocity ωᵇ_ab defined by ω̂ᵇ = R_ab⁻¹ Ṙ_ab: the spin as seen in the instantaneous body frame.
atoms.feynman: The same spin as described by a rider on the merry-go-round, using “forward” and “left” of their own seat.
atoms.visual: Second orange arrow ωᵇ drawn in the blue body axes with 🧍 tag; numbers from the blue skew grid.

atoms.label: Eq (2.50)
atoms.idea: ω̂ᵇ = R⁻¹ω̂ˢR, i.e. ωᵇ = R⁻¹ωˢ: the body spin vector is the spatial one rotated into the current body frame.
atoms.feynman: Ground and rider point at the same physical spin axis; they just name its direction in their own words.
atoms.visual: Overlay: both orange arrows coincide in 3D (lime “same axis”) while their two number panels differ; rotating the slate numbers by Rᵀ reproduces the blue numbers.

atoms.label: Eq (2.51)
atoms.idea: Point velocity in spatial coordinates: v_qa = ω̂ˢ R q_b = ωˢ × q_a.
atoms.feynman: Every sticker on the spinning globe moves sideways to the spin axis, faster the farther it is from it.
atoms.visual: Many pink points with velocity arrows; each equals ωˢ × q_a (cross drawn with a faint parallelogram); arrows vanish on the axis.

atoms.label: Eq (2.52)
atoms.idea: In body coordinates: v_qb = Rᵀ v_qa = ωᵇ × q_b; together Eqs (2.51)–(2.52) give every particle’s velocity from ωˢ or ωᵇ.
atoms.feynman: The rider describes the same sticker speeds using their own forward/left/up.
atoms.visual: Body-camera toggle: the camera rides with B; arrows are now computed as ωᵇ × q_b and look identical in 3D.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.10 and Example 2.4: a one-joint arm rotating about z has ωˢ = ωᵇ = (0, 0, θ̇). Subsection 2.4.2 begins: a general trajectory g_ab(t) ∈ SE(3).

atoms.label: Fig 2.10
atoms.idea: Figure 2.10: a single revolute link turning by θ(t).
atoms.feynman: A clock hand.
atoms.visual: One orange joint at the origin, blue link, dial θ(t) playing over time.

atoms.label: Ex 2.4
atoms.idea: Example 2.4: the 1-DOF arm’s orientation is R(t) = Rz(θ(t)).
atoms.feynman: The clock hand’s attitude is just “turned by θ about the face’s axis”.
atoms.visual: The 3×3 grid shows the z-rotation pattern ticking with θ(t).

atoms.label: Ex 2.4 spatial
atoms.idea: Spatial: ṘRᵀ = θ̇ ẑ-hat, so ωˢ = (0, 0, θ̇).
atoms.feynman: The ground sees the hand spinning about the dial’s axle at rate θ̇.
atoms.visual: Product ṘRᵀ computed live: only two mirrored cells ±θ̇ are non-zero; the orange ωˢ arrow points along blue z with length θ̇.

atoms.label: Ex 2.4 body
atoms.idea: Body: RᵀṘ gives the same ωᵇ = (0, 0, θ̇), since the spin axis is z in both frames.
atoms.feynman: Spinning about the axle looks the same from the ground and from the hand, because the axle is shared.
atoms.visual: ωᵇ arrow appears on the link’s own z axis and matches ωˢ (lime) — a case where the two agree.

atoms.idea: Subsection 2.4.2 heading: Rigid body velocity.
General case: g_ab(t) ∈ SE(3) is the trajectory of body frame B relative to inertial A. (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: Now the globe both spins and flies across the room.
atoms.visual: Unpin the body: drag it in both position and orientation; a trail is recorded.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: ġg⁻¹ is shaped exactly like a twist: the spatial velocity V̂ˢ = ġg⁻¹, Vˢ = (−ṘRᵀp + ṗ, (ṘRᵀ)∨) (Eq 2.53); point velocities are v_qa = ωˢ × q_a + vˢ (Eq 2.54). vˢ is the velocity of the (possibly imaginary) body point currently at the spatial origin; the screw of Vˢ gives the instantaneous axis.

atoms.label: ġg⁻¹
atoms.idea: As with rotations, ġ alone isn’t useful but ġg⁻¹ and g⁻¹ġ are: ġg⁻¹ = [ṘRᵀ, −ṘRᵀp + ṗ; 0 0], which has the shape of a twist.
atoms.feynman: Measuring change relative to where you are turns a messy change into a clean instruction.
atoms.visual: The raw ġ grid (coral badge) multiplied by g⁻¹ becomes a grid with a skew block and a zero bottom row — the twist shape lights lime.

atoms.label: Eq (2.53)
atoms.idea: Spatial velocity V̂ˢ_ab = ġ_ab g_ab⁻¹ ∈ se(3), with coordinates vˢ = −Ṙ Rᵀ p + ṗ and ωˢ = (ṘRᵀ)∨.
atoms.feynman: The room’s single six-number summary of how the whole body is moving right now.
atoms.visual: 6-bar Vˢ (teal vˢ, orange ωˢ) tagged 🌍, updating as you drag.

atoms.label: Eq (2.54)
atoms.idea: For a body point q_a(t) = g q_b: v_qa = ġ g⁻¹ q_a = V̂ˢ q_a = ωˢ × q_a + vˢ.
atoms.feynman: Any crumb’s speed = the spin-sweep at its location plus one shared sliding term.
atoms.visual: Each pink point’s velocity arrow is drawn as orange ωˢ × q_a plus teal vˢ tip-to-tail; it matches the finite-difference velocity (lime).

atoms.idea: Interpreting Vˢ: ωˢ is the spin seen from the fixed frame; vˢ is not how fast the body frame’s origin moves, but how fast the (perhaps imaginary) body point that is currently sitting at the fixed origin moves.
atoms.feynman: Stand still at a spot in the room and imagine the tumbling box were huge enough to pass through you: vˢ is how fast the piece of box going through your spot is moving.
atoms.visual: The blue body grows a faint ghost extension (an infinite rigid sheet) that reaches the slate origin; a ghost point 👻 there shows a teal arrow equal to vˢ, while the body’s own origin has a different (coral) velocity arrow.

atoms.idea: A friendlier reading: convert Vˢ into its screw, and you get the current screw axis, pitch and size of the motion as seen from the fixed frame.
atoms.feynman: At each instant the tumbling box is momentarily being screwed along some bolt; Vˢ tells you which bolt.
atoms.visual: A gold instantaneous screw axis (from the 6 bars via pitch/axis formulas) floats near the body and shifts as you change the motion; points on it slide only along it.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Body velocity V̂ᵇ = g⁻¹ġ, Vᵇ = (Rᵀṗ, (RᵀṘ)∨) (Eq 2.55); v_qb = ωᵇ × q_b + vᵇ (Eq 2.56); vᵇ is the body-origin velocity in body axes. The two are related by conjugation; in coordinates Vˢ = [R p̂R; 0 R] Vᵇ (Eq 2.57), defining the adjoint Ad_g (Eq 2.58).

atoms.label: Eq (2.55)
atoms.idea: Body velocity V̂ᵇ_ab = g⁻¹ġ = [RᵀṘ, Rᵀṗ; 0 0], coordinates vᵇ = Rᵀṗ, ωᵇ = (RᵀṘ)∨.
atoms.feynman: The rider’s six-number summary of how the vehicle is moving, in the rider’s own forward/left/up.
atoms.visual: 6-bar Vᵇ tagged 🧍 beside Vˢ; a body-camera toggle shows the scene from B.

atoms.label: Eq (2.56)
atoms.idea: Point velocity in body coordinates: v_qb = g⁻¹ v_qa = V̂ᵇ q_b = ωᵇ × q_b + vᵇ.
atoms.feynman: The rider computes each crumb’s speed the same way: spin-sweep plus a shared slide, all in rider words.
atoms.visual: In body-camera view, each pink arrow equals orange ωᵇ × q_b plus teal vᵇ.

atoms.idea: vᵇ is the velocity of the body-frame origin (relative to the spatial frame) expressed in current body axes; ωᵇ is the angular velocity in body axes. It is not velocity relative to the body frame, which is zero.
atoms.feynman: A car’s speedometer and the “turning left” feeling: the car’s own motion, described from the driver’s seat.
atoms.visual: A ⏱️ speedometer glyph at the body origin reads vᵇ (teal arrow along body axes); a gyro glyph reads ωᵇ.

atoms.label: Eq (2.57)
atoms.idea: Relation: V̂ˢ = g V̂ᵇ g⁻¹; in components ωˢ = Rωᵇ and vˢ = p × (Rωᵇ) + Rvᵇ, i.e. Vˢ = [R p̂R; 0 R] Vᵇ.
atoms.feynman: The room and the rider describe the same motion; translate the rider’s words by turning them and adding the lever effect of where the rider sits.
atoms.visual: Arrow-level animation: rotate Vᵇ bars by R (orange), then add the teal p × (Rωᵇ) lever term to the linear part; result equals the measured Vˢ bars (lime).

atoms.label: Eq (2.58)
atoms.idea: The 6×6 matrix moving twists between frames is the adjoint Ad_g = [R p̂R; 0 R] for g = (p, R).
atoms.feynman: A translator for six-number motion descriptions between two observers.
atoms.visual: 6×6 grid with two orange R blocks on the diagonal, a teal p̂R block top-right, slate zeros bottom-left; drag the observer frame and the blocks update.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Ad_g maps body to spatial twist coordinates; its inverse is Ad_{g⁻¹} = [Rᵀ −Rᵀp̂; 0 Rᵀ] (Exercise 14). Lemma 2.13: g ξ̂ g⁻¹ has coordinates Ad_g ξ. Frame-free spatial and body velocities (Eqs 2.59–2.60) satisfy Vˢ = Ad_g Vᵇ (Eq 2.61). Example 2.5 begins.

atoms.label: Ad⁻¹
atoms.idea: Ad_g maps body to spatial coordinates; it is invertible with (Ad_g)⁻¹ = [Rᵀ, −Rᵀp̂; 0, Rᵀ] = Ad_{g⁻¹}.
atoms.feynman: Translating back is the same as using the reverse observer’s translator.
atoms.visual: Inverse button: the 6×6 grid flips into the reversed-observer grid; Ad_g · Ad_{g⁻¹} collapses to I₆ (lime).

atoms.label: Lemma 2.13
atoms.idea: Lemma 2.13: for any twist ξ̂ and g ∈ SE(3), g ξ̂ g⁻¹ is a twist with coordinates Ad_g ξ.
atoms.feynman: Moving a bolt (or moving yourself relative to it) gives another bolt, and the translator tells you which.
atoms.visual: Gold twist axis on the body; apply a rigid move g; matrix route g ξ̂ g⁻¹ and coordinate route Ad_g ξ produce the same new gold axis (lime overlap).

atoms.label: Eqs (2.59)–(2.61)
atoms.idea: Frame-free notation: for configuration g, Vˢ = (ġg⁻¹)∨ = (−ṘRᵀp + ṗ, (ṘRᵀ)∨) and Vᵇ = (g⁻¹ġ)∨ = (Rᵀṗ, (RᵀṘ)∨), with Vˢ = Ad_g Vᵇ.
atoms.feynman: Two standard ways to report motion — the room’s and the rider’s — always related by the same translator.
atoms.visual: Two 6-bar meters (🌍 Vˢ, 🧍 Vᵇ) wired through the 6×6 Ad grid; drag the body and both update consistently.

atoms.label: Ex 2.5
atoms.idea: Example 2.5: a 1-DOF manipulator (Fig 2.11) with g(t) = [Rz(θ), (−l₂ sin θ, l₁ + l₂ cos θ, l₀); 0 1]; compute Vˢ.
atoms.feynman: A carousel arm with a seat at its end, lifted to height l₀.
atoms.visual: Fig 2.11 scene: orange joint at distance l₁ from A, blue arm of length l₂ to frame B at height l₀; θ plays over time.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.11; Example 2.5 results: Vˢ = (l₁θ̇, 0, 0, 0, 0, θ̇) — the velocity of the body point at A’s origin — and Vᵇ = (−l₂θ̇, 0, 0, 0, 0, θ̇) — the B-origin velocity in B axes. Subsection 2.4.3 on screw-motion velocity begins.

atoms.label: Fig 2.11
atoms.idea: Figure 2.11: a link rotating about a fixed vertical axis offset l₁ from A, with frame B at radius l₂ and height l₀.
atoms.feynman: A carousel seat on an arm.
atoms.visual: Fig 2.11 rendered with labels as single symbols only (l₀, l₁, l₂, θ).

atoms.label: Ex 2.5 spatial
atoms.idea: vˢ = (l₁θ̇, 0, 0), ωˢ = (0, 0, θ̇); vˢ is exactly the velocity of a body point passing through A’s origin.
atoms.feynman: If the carousel arm were long enough to sweep through where you stand, that sweeping piece would move at l₁θ̇.
atoms.visual: Ghost extension of the arm reaches A’s origin; the 👻 point there shows a teal arrow of length l₁θ̇ along x that equals the vˢ bars (lime).

atoms.label: Ex 2.5 body
atoms.idea: vᵇ = Rᵀṗ = (−l₂θ̇, 0, 0), ωᵇ = (0, 0, θ̇): the B-origin always moves along its own −x, at a speed set by the arm length l₂.
atoms.feynman: Sitting on the carousel seat, you always feel yourself moving straight “backward-sideways” at the same speed.
atoms.visual: Body-camera view: the speedometer arrow at B is fixed along −x_B with length l₂θ̇ for all θ.

atoms.idea: Subsection 2.4.3 heading: Velocity of a screw motion.
Example 2.5 was a motion generated by a screw, exp(ξ̂θ). (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: That carousel was a thread-less bolt in disguise.
atoms.visual: The gold screw axis of the joint appears on the Fig 2.11 scene.
atoms.beat: 🔩 a screw’s velocity is its twist

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: For g_ab(θ) = exp(ξ̂θ)g_ab(0), d/dt exp(ξ̂θ) = ξ̂θ̇ exp(ξ̂θ) gives V̂ˢ = ξ̂θ̇ — the spatial velocity is the screw’s twist — and Vᵇ = Ad_{g_ab(0)⁻¹} ξ θ̇, constant in the body. Subsection 2.4.4: Proposition 2.14, Vˢ_ac = Vˢ_ab + Ad_{g_ab} Vˢ_bc.

atoms.idea: Compared with Example 2.3, Vˢ of Example 2.5 equals ξ when θ̇ = 1; consider the general g_ab(θ) = exp(ξ̂θ)g_ab(0).
atoms.feynman: The carousel’s room-velocity was just its bolt recipe.
atoms.visual: 6-bar Vˢ and the twist card ξ side by side: with θ̇ = 1 they are identical (lime).
atoms.beat: 🔩 a screw’s velocity is its twist

atoms.label: V̂ˢ = ξ̂θ̇
atoms.idea: Using d/dt exp(ξ̂θ) = ξ̂θ̇ exp(ξ̂θ) (Exercise 8), ġg⁻¹ = ξ̂θ̇ — the spatial velocity is exactly the screw’s twist scaled by θ̇, whatever the starting pose.
atoms.feynman: A bolt being turned: the room sees the same bolt-recipe at every moment; only the turning speed scales it.
atoms.visual: Constant gold screw axis; any blue body attached anywhere moves along it; Vˢ bars stay parallel to ξ and scale with the θ̇ knob, independent of the body’s start pose (drag g(0): Vˢ unchanged).
atoms.beat: 🔩 a screw’s velocity is its twist

atoms.label: Vᵇ = Ad⁻¹ξθ̇
atoms.idea: Body velocity: V̂ᵇ = g⁻¹ġ = g_ab(0)⁻¹ ξ̂ g_ab(0) θ̇, so Vᵇ = Ad_{g_ab(0)⁻¹} ξ θ̇.
atoms.feynman: The rider sees the same bolt, but described from where they were bolted on at the start.
atoms.visual: Body-camera view: Vᵇ bars computed as the 6×6 Ad of g(0)⁻¹ times ξ; dragging g(0) changes Vᵇ but not Vˢ.
atoms.beat: 🔩 a screw’s velocity is its twist

atoms.idea: For θ̇ = 1, Vᵇ is constant in the moving body; its direction is set by the initial configuration via the adjoint; if g_ab(0) = I then Vˢ = Vᵇ = ξθ̇.
atoms.feynman: If you’re bolted on right at the room’s corner, you and the room describe the bolt the same way.
atoms.visual: Snap g(0) to the identity: the 🌍 and 🧍 bars become identical (lime).
atoms.beat: 🔩 a screw’s velocity is its twist

atoms.idea: Subsection 2.4.4 heading: Coordinate transformations.
Just as poses compose, velocities between frame pairs combine to give the velocity of one frame relative to a third.
atoms.feynman: A passenger walking on a moving train: their speed over the ground combines the two.
atoms.visual: Three frames A (slate), B (blue, on a moving cart), C (teal, moving on B).

atoms.label: Prop 2.14
atoms.idea: Proposition 2.14: Vˢ_ac = Vˢ_ab + Ad_{g_ab} Vˢ_bc.
atoms.feynman: Ground speed of the walking passenger = the train’s motion + the passenger’s motion translated into ground terms.
atoms.visual: Two twist arrows: Vˢ_ab (B’s motion) and Ad_{g_ab}Vˢ_bc (C-on-B motion re-expressed in A) add tip-to-tail into Vˢ_ac, which matches the measured motion of C (lime).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Proof of Prop 2.14 via g_ac = g_ab g_bc and the product rule; Proposition 2.15: Vᵇ_ac = Ad_{g_bc⁻¹} Vᵇ_ab + Vᵇ_bc. With A, B fixed relative to each other, Vˢ_ac = Ad_{g_ab}Vˢ_bc (Eq 2.62) and Vᵇ_ac = Vᵇ_bc (Eq 2.63). Moving a screw by g changes its twist to Ad_g ξ = g ξ̂ g⁻¹ (Eq 2.64).

atoms.label: Prop 2.14 proof
atoms.idea: Proof: g_ac = g_ab g_bc; by the product rule ġ_ac g_ac⁻¹ = ġ_ab g_ab⁻¹ + g_ab(ġ_bc g_bc⁻¹)g_ab⁻¹; converting to coordinates with Lemma 2.13 gives the result.
atoms.feynman: Change of the whole chain = change of the first link + change of the second link seen through the first.
atoms.visual: Staircase: tile 1 chain A→B→C; tile 2 the product-rule split as two colored terms; tile 3 the second term passes through the Ad grid and lands in A coordinates.

atoms.label: Prop 2.15
atoms.idea: Proposition 2.15: body velocities chain as Vᵇ_ac = Ad_{g_bc⁻¹} Vᵇ_ab + Vᵇ_bc (proof by the same chain rule).
atoms.feynman: The passenger’s own feeling of motion = their walking + the train’s motion re-described from the passenger’s seat.
atoms.visual: Body-camera on C: the two contributions shown as arrows in C’s axes and summed.

atoms.label: Eqs (2.62)–(2.63)
atoms.idea: If A and B never move with respect to one another: Vˢ_ac = Ad_{g_ab}Vˢ_bc and Vᵇ_ac = Vᵇ_bc — body velocity doesn’t depend on which inertial frame measures it.
atoms.feynman: Two people standing still in a room describe a runner differently, but the runner’s own speedometer reads the same for both.
atoms.visual: Freeze B relative to A (two slate frames): spatial bars differ by Ad, body bars identical (lime).

atoms.label: Eq (2.64)
atoms.idea: Applying a fixed rigid motion g to a screw (ġ = 0) changes its twist to ξ′ = Ad_g ξ, i.e. ξ̂′ = g ξ̂ g⁻¹ — how joint axes move.
atoms.feynman: Carry a door, hinge and all, to a new spot: the new hinge recipe is the old recipe translated by the move.
atoms.visual: Drag a rigid move g applied to an orange joint axis; the new gold axis is drawn from Ad_g ξ and coincides with the physically moved axis (lime).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.12; Eq (2.64) will track joint twists as robots move. Example 2.6: for a two-link mechanism, Vˢ_ac = Vˢ_ab + Ad_{g_ab}Vˢ_bc yields a sum of two joint contributions, each linear in its joint rate.

atoms.label: Fig 2.12
atoms.idea: Figure 2.12: a 2-DOF arm — joint θ₁ at frame B (offset l₀ from A) and joint θ₂ at C (distance l₁ along the first link).
atoms.feynman: A desk lamp with a base swivel and an elbow.
atoms.visual: Two orange joints with dials θ₁, θ₂, blue links l₀ and l₁, frames A, B, C.

atoms.idea: Moving twists with Ad is crucial later, to track joint axes as a robot moves.
atoms.feynman: When the shoulder turns, the elbow’s hinge goes with it — we need to know where it went.
atoms.visual: Turn θ₁: the second joint’s gold axis rides along, its coordinates updated by Ad.

atoms.label: Ex 2.6
atoms.idea: Example 2.6: each joint is a screw: Vˢ_ab = (0,0,0,0,0,1)θ̇₁ and Vˢ_bc = (l₁,0,0,0,0,1)θ̇₂.
atoms.feynman: Each joint, by itself, is a simple spin recipe.
atoms.visual: Each joint shows its own 6-bar card scaled by its rate knob.

atoms.label: Ex 2.6 Ad
atoms.idea: Compute Ad_{g_ab} = [R_ab, (0,0,l₀)^R_ab; 0, R_ab].
atoms.feynman: The translator from the elbow’s view to the ground’s view depends on how the shoulder is turned.
atoms.visual: The 6×6 grid for g_ab updates with θ₁.

atoms.label: Ex 2.6 result
atoms.idea: Prop 2.14 gives Vˢ_ac = (0,0,0,0,0,1)θ̇₁ + (l₁cos θ₁, l₁ sin θ₁, 0, 0, 0, 1)θ̇₂: one contribution per joint, adding linearly.
atoms.feynman: The lamp head’s motion is “what the base swivel does” plus “what the elbow does”, just added.
atoms.visual: Two colored twist columns (one per joint) scaled by θ̇₁ and θ̇₂ stack into the total; the second column swings with θ₁. A Jacobian icon previews Chapter 3.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Lemma 2.16: Vᵇ_ab = −Vˢ_ba and Vᵇ_ab = −Ad_{g_ba}Vᵇ_ba. Section 2.5: wrenches and reciprocal screws. A wrench F = (f, τ) ∈ R⁶ depends on the frame; paired with a body twist it gives instantaneous work δW = V·F = v·f + ω·τ and net work as its time integral.

atoms.label: Lemma 2.16
atoms.idea: Lemma 2.16: Vᵇ_ab = −Vˢ_ba and Vᵇ_ab = −Ad_{g_ba}Vᵇ_ba (proof left as an exercise).
atoms.feynman: How I see you move is the reverse of how you see me move.
atoms.visual: Swap-roles button: the frame doing the watching and the frame being watched trade places; the bars flip sign (coral → lime after the minus).

atoms.idea: Section 2.5 heading: Wrenches and Reciprocal Screws.
Forces and moments on rigid bodies lead to screw systems and reciprocal screws.
atoms.feynman: Now pushes instead of motions.
atoms.visual: The orange motion arrows fade and purple push arrows appear on the blue body.

atoms.idea: Subsection 2.5.1 heading: Wrenches.

atoms.label: wrench
atoms.idea: A generalized force is a linear force f plus a moment τ at a point, stacked as F = (f, τ) ∈ R⁶: a wrench.
atoms.feynman: A spanner on a bolt both pushes and twists.
atoms.visual: Purple straight arrow f and purple curled arrow τ at a teal contact point; a 6-bar F meter (f bars, τ bars).

atoms.idea: F’s numbers depend on the frame: F_b = (f_b, τ_b) is applied at B’s origin with components in B.
atoms.feynman: The same push is described differently by someone standing elsewhere or facing another way.
atoms.visual: A teal frame B sits at the application point; the 6 bars are read in B’s axes.

atoms.label: δW
atoms.idea: With body twist Vᵇ_ab and wrench F_b both in B, instantaneous work is δW = Vᵇ·F_b = v·f + ω·τ.
atoms.feynman: Work = push × how far it moved along the push + twist × how much it turned along the twist.
atoms.visual: Play a twist on the body; a power gauge shows v·f (teal-purple) plus ω·τ (orange-purple) as two stacked bars.

atoms.label: W
atoms.idea: Net work over [t₁, t₂]: W = ∫ Vᵇ·F_b dt.
atoms.feynman: Add up all the little bits of effort over the whole trip.
atoms.visual: The power gauge feeds a work tank that fills over time.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.13. Equivalent wrenches do the same work for every motion; equating work gives F_c = Adᵀ_{g_bc} F_b (Eq 2.65): the force is rotated and an extra torque −p_bc × f_b appears (Eq 2.66). Wrenches may also be expressed in a frame outside the body.

atoms.label: Fig 2.13
atoms.idea: Figure 2.13: wrench F at contact frame B, object frame C and inertial frame A.
atoms.feynman: A finger pushing a cup at its rim; the cup’s centre; the table corner.
atoms.visual: Three frames: teal contact B with purple F, blue object frame C, slate A away from the object.

atoms.label: equivalent wrench
atoms.idea: Two wrenches are equivalent if they do the same work for every rigid motion; this lets us re-express a wrench at another point and frame, e.g. from contact frame B to object frame C.
atoms.feynman: Pushing a door at the handle or pushing harder near the hinge can feel the same to the door.
atoms.visual: Test-twist mode: randomly wiggle the object; work gauges for F_b (at B) and F_c (at C) read identical for every wiggle (lime).

atoms.label: Eq (2.65)
atoms.idea: Equate work: Vᵇ_ac·F_c = Vᵇ_ab·F_b = (Ad_{g_bc}Vᵇ_ac)·F_b = Vᵇ_ac·(Adᵀ_{g_bc}F_b); since Vᵇ_ac is arbitrary, F_c = Adᵀ_{g_bc} F_b.
atoms.feynman: If two pushes cost the same effort under any wiggle you try, they are really one and the same push.
atoms.visual: Staircase: tile 1 equal gauges; tile 2 the Ad grid moves from the twist side to the wrench side as its transpose (grid flips over its diagonal); tile 3 the new purple arrows at C.

atoms.label: Eq (2.66)
atoms.idea: Expanded: f_c = R_bcᵀ f_b, τ_c = R_bcᵀ(τ_b − p_bc × f_b) — the force is rotated into C, plus the torque of f_b applied at offset −p_bc.
atoms.feynman: Pushing a seesaw off-centre also twists it — the farther from the middle, the bigger the twist.
atoms.visual: Drag C away from B: the purple force arrow at C stays parallel and equal; a coral extra-torque arc grows as the lever arm p × f.

atoms.idea: A wrench can also be expressed in a frame outside the body, e.g. frame A. (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: You can even describe the push from the table corner, as if the table corner were glued to the cup.
atoms.visual: Drag the reference frame off the object into empty space (slate A).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Wrench in an outside frame A: F_a = Adᵀ_{g_ba}F_b, with application point at A’s origin. Wrenches add only once moved to a common frame/point. Body and spatial wrenches satisfy Fᵇ = Adᵀ_g Fˢ (Eq 2.67), and δW = Vᵇ·Fᵇ = Vˢ·Fˢ. Example 2.7 (grasp preview) begins.

atoms.label: F_a
atoms.idea: F_a = Adᵀ_{g_ba} F_b is the equivalent wrench applied at A’s origin as if A were glued to the object — not merely F_b’s components rewritten in A axes, since the application point moved.
atoms.feynman: Describing a push “from the table corner” means imagining a rod from the corner to the cup and asking what push-and-twist at the corner does the same job.
atoms.visual: A faint rigid rod links slate A to the object; the purple wrench redrawn at A’s origin includes a coral lever torque. A comparison ghost (just re-axed numbers, no lever term) is marked coral ✗.

atoms.idea: To total several wrenches, first re-express every one at a single common point and frame (say the centre of mass or a fixed frame), then add — this is the reason re-expressing a wrench also moves its point of application.
atoms.feynman: You can only add pushes after asking what each one does at the same spot.
atoms.visual: Three purple finger pushes at different points; a “gather” button slides each to the blue object frame O (each growing its coral lever torque), then they stack into one net wrench pair.

atoms.label: body/spatial wrench
atoms.idea: A net wrench has a body representation F_b (at B’s origin, in B axes) and a spatial one (equivalent wrench in A’s frame), mirroring body and spatial velocities.
atoms.feynman: The cup-holder’s description and the room’s description of the same total push.
atoms.visual: Two 6-bar wrench meters tagged 🧍 (body) and 🌍 (spatial), both describing one purple wrench pair.

atoms.label: Eq (2.67)
atoms.idea: Frame-free: Fᵇ = Adᵀ_g Fˢ; power is the same in either description: δW = Vᵇ·Fᵇ = Vˢ·Fˢ (exercise).
atoms.feynman: However you describe the push and the motion, the effort spent is a fact both observers agree on.
atoms.visual: Two power gauges — one from (🧍 twist · 🧍 wrench), one from (🌍 twist · 🌍 wrench) — always read the same (lime), while all four bar sets differ.

atoms.label: Ex 2.7
atoms.idea: Example 2.7: multifingered grasp preview (Fig 2.14); F_ci is the wrench from finger i in its contact frame C_i. (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: Two fingers pinching a cracker.
atoms.visual: Fig 2.14 scene: object frame O, contact frames C1, C2 on its sides, finger glyphs S1, S2.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.14; the net grasp wrench is F_o = Σ Adᵀ_{g_{c_i o}} F_ci, the basic grasping calculation. Section 2.5.2: Poinsot’s theorem, the dual of Chasles; a screw (l, h, M) defines a wrench: force M along l and torque hM about l (Eq 2.68).

atoms.label: Fig 2.14
atoms.idea: Figure 2.14: object frame O between two contact frames C1, C2 touched by fingers S1, S2.
atoms.feynman: A sandwich held between two fingers.
atoms.visual: Blue object with frame O, teal contact frames C1, C2, orange finger tips S1, S2.

atoms.label: F_o = Σ
atoms.idea: Net wrench in O: F_o = Σᵢ Adᵀ_{g_{oc_i}⁻¹} F_ci — the basic grasp calculation for the effect of contact forces.
atoms.feynman: Add what each finger does to the sandwich’s middle.
atoms.visual: Each finger’s purple push travels to O with its lever torque; the two stack into the net (gold if it balances to zero, else purple arrow pair).

atoms.idea: Subsection 2.5.2 heading: Screw coordinates for a wrench.
Poinsot’s theorem mirrors Chasles: any wrench can be swapped for a push along some line together with a twist about the same line.
atoms.feynman: Every motion is a screw (Chasles); every push is a screwdriver (Poinsot).
atoms.visual: Twist-screw thumbnail (orange) and wrench-screw thumbnail (purple) side by side with a ⇄ glyph.

atoms.label: Eq (2.68)
atoms.idea: Wrench along screw S = (l = {q + λω}, h, M): F = M(ω, −ω × q + hω) for finite h; F = M(0, ω) (pure torque) if h = ∞.
atoms.feynman: A screwdriver pushes along its shaft and twists about it; the farther the shaft is from your reference point, the more extra twist it seems to make there.
atoms.visual: Draw the gold line l; slider M sets the purple force along it, slider h adds a purple torque hM about it; 6-bar F shows f = Mω and τ = M(−ω×q + hω), with the −ω×q part in coral as the offset effect.
atoms.beat: 🪛 push along + twist about a line

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: F is a spatial wrench; −ω × q accounts for the axis offset. Theorem 2.17 (Poinsot) proved constructively: pure torque gives infinite pitch; otherwise M = ‖f‖, ω = f/M, h = fᵀτ/‖f‖², q = f × τ/‖f‖² (non-unique along the axis). Wrench pitch (Eq 2.69) and axis (Eq 2.70).

atoms.idea: The −ω×q term encodes the offset between the screw axis and A’s origin; F is the spatial wrench (all in frame A).
atoms.feynman: Push a door far from where you stand and, from your spot, it also looks like a twist.
atoms.visual: Drag q away from the origin: f stays the same, τ grows its coral offset part; at q on the origin it vanishes.
atoms.beat: 🪛 push along + twist about a line

atoms.idea: To get screw coordinates of a wrench, solve Eq (2.68) for ω, q, h, M given F = (f, τ).
atoms.feynman: Given a total push, find the one screwdriver that does it.
atoms.visual: Wrench-in, screw-out machine icon; F bars feed in.

atoms.label: Thm 2.17
atoms.idea: Theorem 2.17 (Poinsot): whatever set of wrenches acts on a body, one line exists such that a push along it plus a twist about it has exactly the same effect.
atoms.feynman: However many people push and twist a table, it is as if one person were using one giant screwdriver on it.
atoms.visual: Throw many random purple forces/torques on the blue body; a “reduce” button collapses them into a single gold axis with one force arrow and one torque arc (lime: same work for every test wiggle).

atoms.label: Thm 2.17 case 1
atoms.idea: Proof (F ≠ 0). Pure torque f = 0: M = ‖τ‖, ω = τ/M, h = ∞.
atoms.feynman: If nobody pushes, only twists, it is a pure twist — infinite pitch.
atoms.visual: Staircase tile 1: zero force bars; the axis passes through the origin along τ with an ∞ badge.

atoms.label: Thm 2.17 case 2
atoms.idea: f ≠ 0: M = ‖f‖, ω = f/M; solve M(q × ω + hω) = τ: h = fᵀτ/‖f‖², q = f × τ/‖f‖²; any q + λω works too.
atoms.feynman: Split the twist into a part along the push (that’s the screwdriver turn) and a part across it (that tells you where the screwdriver shaft must be).
atoms.visual: Staircase tile 2: τ splits into lime along-f part (gives h) and slate across-f part (gives q via f×τ/‖f‖²); the gold axis appears through q along f; sliding q along it changes nothing.

atoms.label: Eq (2.69)
atoms.idea: Wrench pitch h = fᵀτ/‖f‖²: torque per unit force along the axis; infinite if f = 0.
atoms.feynman: How much the screwdriver twists for each unit of push.
atoms.visual: Pitch readout and a lime projection bar of τ on f.

atoms.label: Eq (2.70)
atoms.idea: Wrench axis: line along f through f × τ/‖f‖² (f ≠ 0), or along τ through the origin (f = 0).
atoms.feynman: Where the screwdriver shaft must sit.
atoms.visual: Gold axis line drawn from the formula; a gold dot at f×τ/‖f‖².

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Wrench magnitude ‖f‖ (or ‖τ‖) (Eq 2.71); duality: zero-pitch twist = pure rotation, zero-pitch wrench = pure force. Section 2.5.3: a wrench is reciprocal to a twist if F·V = 0; Definition 2.3 (reciprocal screws); the reciprocal product S₁⊙S₂ = M₁M₂((h₁+h₂)cos α − d sin α) (Eq 2.72); Proposition 2.18.

atoms.label: Eq (2.71)
atoms.idea: Wrench magnitude M = ‖f‖ if f ≠ 0, else ‖τ‖.
atoms.feynman: How hard the screwdriver pushes — or, if it only twists, how hard it twists.
atoms.visual: Magnitude bar equals the purple force arrow length (or the torque arc size when f = 0).

atoms.idea: Duality: pitch 0 means pure spinning for a twist but pure pushing for a wrench — the linear and angular halves trade roles.
atoms.feynman: A hinge spins without sliding; a pure push shoves without twisting — they are mirror twins.
atoms.visual: Side-by-side panels with identical gold axes and pitch 0: left an orange spin arc (twist), right a purple straight arrow (wrench); toggling pitch to ∞ swaps to a slide and a pure torque.

atoms.idea: Subsection 2.5.3 heading: Reciprocal screws.

atoms.label: reciprocal
atoms.idea: Twist·wrench is instantaneous power; F is reciprocal to V if F·V = 0.
atoms.feynman: Pushing on a sliding door straight into its track does no work: the push and the motion are “reciprocal”.
atoms.visual: Orange twist and purple wrench on a body; power gauge; when it reads exactly 0 the pair glows lime.

atoms.label: Def 2.3
atoms.idea: Definition 2.3: call S₁ and S₂ reciprocal when moving along S₁ does zero work against a wrench along S₂.
atoms.feynman: Two bolts are reciprocal if turning along one never fights a screwdriver on the other.
atoms.visual: Two gold axes S₁ (orange motion) and S₂ (purple push) with the power gauge.

atoms.label: Eq (2.72)
atoms.idea: Classical reciprocal product: with d the shortest distance between the axes (along unit common normal n) and α = atan2((ω₁×ω₂)·n, ω₁·ω₂), S₁⊙S₂ = M₁M₂((h₁+h₂)cos α − d sin α).
atoms.feynman: Whether two bolts fight depends on how far apart they are, how skewed, and how coarse their threads are.
atoms.visual: Teal common-normal segment of length d between the two gold axes; an α arc; three readouts (h₁+h₂, d, α) feed the formula live; dragging axes apart/skewing them changes the product.

atoms.label: Prop 2.18
atoms.idea: Proposition 2.18: S₁, S₂ are reciprocal iff S₁⊙S₂ = 0.
atoms.feynman: The fight-meter reads zero exactly when the bolts never fight.
atoms.visual: The geometric formula readout and the power gauge V·F move together and hit zero at the same moment (lime).

atoms.label: Prop 2.18 proof
atoms.idea: Proof sketch, both pitches finite (remaining cases left to the reader): write the S₁ motion as a twist V and the S₂ push as a wrench F. (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: Write both bolts down as six numbers and compute the work.
atoms.visual: Staircase header: V (orange bars) and F (purple bars) cards.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.15; proof of Prop 2.18 by computing V·F with q₂ = q₁ + dn, giving the reciprocal product. In twist coordinates V₁⊙V₂ = v₁ᵀω₂ + v₂ᵀω₁. Reciprocal screws help find motions a grasp cannot resist.

atoms.label: Fig 2.15
atoms.idea: Figure 2.15: screws S₁, S₂ with closest points q₁, q₂, distance d and angle α between directions ω₁, ω₂.
atoms.feynman: Two pencils floating at a skew, with the shortest string joining them.
atoms.visual: Two gold axes, teal shortest segment d, angle arc α.

atoms.label: Prop 2.18 proof
atoms.idea: V = M₁(q₁×ω₁ + h₁ω₁, ω₁), F = M₂(ω₂, q₂×ω₂ + h₂ω₂) with q₂ = q₁ + dn at closest points; expanding V·F, the q₁ triple products cancel and what remains is M₁M₂((h₁+h₂)cos α − d sin α).
atoms.feynman: Most of the bookkeeping cancels out; only “thread coarseness × alignment” and “distance × skew” survive.
atoms.visual: Staircase: tile 1 the four terms appear as colored chips; tile 2 the two q₁ chips annihilate (puff); tile 3 the d·n chip becomes −d sin α and the pitch chips become (h₁+h₂)cos α; tile 4 equals the gauge.

atoms.label: V₁⊙V₂
atoms.idea: In twist coordinates the reciprocal product is V₁⊙V₂ = v₁ᵀω₂ + v₂ᵀω₁ (similarly for wrenches).
atoms.feynman: Swap the halves of one card and take the dot product.
atoms.visual: Two 6-bar cards; the second card’s halves swap places (animated) and a dot-product bar computes the same number as the geometric formula.

atoms.idea: Uses: in grasping, the finger wrenches are constraining screws; any twist reciprocal to all of them is a motion the fingers cannot stop. (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: If fingers only push straight in, the object can still slide along the direction none of them push against.
atoms.visual: Fingers on a blue body; any lime ghost wiggle that does zero work against every finger is played as an “escape”.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Figure 2.16: normal forces on a body. Any screw reciprocal to all applied-wrench screws is an unresisted motion. Screws inherit linear structure from twists (systems of screws), and a screw reciprocal to S₁, S₂ is reciprocal to their combinations, defining the reciprocal screw system.

atoms.label: Fig 2.16
atoms.idea: Figure 2.16: three pure forces F₁, F₂, F₃ acting normally on a rigid body.
atoms.feynman: Three fingertips pressing on a pebble.
atoms.visual: Blue body with three purple normal arrows.

atoms.idea: Chapter 5 treats this in detail; here we preview the analysis with screw systems.
atoms.feynman: A sneak peek at the grasping chapter.
atoms.visual: A ✋ chapter-5 badge on the scene.

atoms.label: Fig 2.16 analysis
atoms.idea: With wrench screws S₁…S_k, any S_f with S_f⊙Sᵢ = 0 for all i is a twist doing no work against every wrench: the forces cannot resist it, so nothing stops the object from instantaneously moving along S_f.
atoms.feynman: If a wiggle never pushes back against any finger, the fingers can’t stop it.
atoms.visual: For the three forces, the scene computes reciprocal twists and plays them as lime ghost wiggles; power gauges against each finger read 0.

atoms.label: system of screws
atoms.idea: Viewing screws as twists makes them a real vector space; a set {S₁…S_k} is a system of screws, scaled and added via their twists.
atoms.feynman: Recipe cards can be mixed: half of this one plus twice that one is another recipe.
atoms.visual: Two orange twist cards with weight sliders; their blend redraws a new gold axis and pitch.

atoms.idea: Reciprocity is linear: reciprocal to S₁ and S₂ means reciprocal to every combination; the set of all screws reciprocal to a system is its reciprocal screw system. (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: If a wiggle doesn’t fight two fingers, it won’t fight any blend of those fingers either.
atoms.visual: Blend the two finger wrenches with sliders; the lime escape wiggle’s gauge stays at 0 for every blend.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: A reciprocal screw system is a linear subspace: for constraint wrenches it gives the allowed motions; for twists it gives wrenches causing no net motion. Proposition 2.19: screw-system dimension plus reciprocal dimension equals 6. For Fig 2.16, at least 3 motions are unresisted.

atoms.idea: Reciprocal systems are linear subspaces: wrenches as constraints → reciprocal = allowed instantaneous motions; twists as motions → reciprocal = wrenches that cause no net motion.
atoms.feynman: Rails decide which way a train can roll; and a train that can only roll along the rails ignores any push straight into the rails.
atoms.visual: Toggle between “purple wrenches given → lime motions found” and “orange motions given → purple pushes that do nothing found”.

atoms.idea: Screw systems also analyse mechanism mobility (next chapter); the key tool follows from twists forming a 6-D linear space.
atoms.feynman: Count how many ways something can still move by counting how many ways it is held.
atoms.visual: A mechanism glyph with a mobility counter.

atoms.label: Prop 2.19
atoms.idea: Proposition 2.19: a screw system of dimension r and its reciprocal system of dimension n always satisfy r + n = 6.
atoms.feynman: Six ways to move in total: every independent way you hold an object takes away exactly one way it can move.
atoms.visual: A 6-cell bar: purple cells for independent constraint wrenches, lime cells for free motions; adding a finger turns one lime cell purple; the bar always has 6 cells.

atoms.label: Fig 2.16 count
atoms.idea: For the three forces of Fig 2.16, at least 3 independent motions are unresisted — more if the forces’ wrenches are dependent.
atoms.feynman: Three fingers can block at most three ways of moving; the other three slip free.
atoms.visual: Three purple cells, three lime cells; make two forces parallel and collinear: a purple cell turns lime (only 2 independent), coral flash.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Summary items 1–3: configurations are g = [R p; 0 1] ∈ SE(3) (also frame-to-frame maps); every g is exp(ξ̂θ) of a twist ξ = (v, ω); twists ↔ screws with pitch, axis and magnitude formulas, pure rotation and translation twists. Item 4 (velocities) begins.

atoms.idea: Section 2.6 heading: Summary.
Key concepts of the chapter follow.
atoms.feynman: Time to tidy the toy box.
atoms.visual: The summary board appears with five dim tiles.

atoms.idea: Item 1: a rigid configuration is g ∈ SE(3), a distance- and angle-preserving map, written homogeneously as [R p; 0 1]; also used between frames.
atoms.feynman: Where the box is and which way it faces, on one card.
atoms.visual: Tile 📦 lights: the 4×4 grid loop from the homogeneous scene.

atoms.idea: Item 2: rigid transformations are exponentials of twists, g = exp(ξ̂θ) with ξ̂ = [ω̂ v; 0 0] and coordinates ξ = (v, ω).
atoms.feynman: Every move is a steady spin-and-slide recipe run for a while.
atoms.visual: Tile 🔩 lights: n tiny steps converging to a helix.

atoms.idea: Item 3: a twist has a screw with pitch ωᵀv/‖ω‖², axis through ω×v/‖ω‖² along ω (or along v through 0), magnitude ‖ω‖ (or ‖v‖); conversely pure rotation about {q + λω} is (−ω×q, ω)θ and pure translation is (v, 0)θ.
atoms.feynman: Every recipe card describes a bolt, and every bolt has a recipe card; hinges and drawers are the two simplest bolts.
atoms.visual: Tile 🔩 also shows a pitch slider snapping between 0 (hinge) and ∞ (drawer).

atoms.idea: Item 4 (start): velocity of g(t) can be given two ways; the spatial velocity is V̂ˢ = ġg⁻¹. (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: Two observers describe the motion.
atoms.visual: Tile 🏃 lights with the 🌍 bar set.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Summary items 4–6: spatial velocity (observer at the reference origin) and body velocity g⁻¹ġ related by Ad_g; chaining rules for velocities; wrenches F = (f, τ), moved by Adᵀ, with spatial and body forms; wrench screw coordinates. Item 7 begins.

atoms.idea: Item 4: Vˢ is the velocity seen by an observer at the reference origin; Vᵇ = (g⁻¹ġ)∨ is the velocity in the instantaneous body frame; Vˢ = Ad_g Vᵇ with Ad_g = [R p̂R; 0 R]; frames chain via Vˢ_ac = Vˢ_ab + Ad_{g_ab}Vˢ_bc and Vᵇ_ac = Ad_{g_bc⁻¹}Vᵇ_ab + Vᵇ_bc.
atoms.feynman: The room and the rider each give a six-number report; a fixed translator converts one to the other, and chains add up like walking on a train.
atoms.visual: Tile 🏃: 🌍 and 🧍 bars linked through the 6×6 Ad grid, plus the A→B→C chain sum.

atoms.idea: Item 5: wrenches F = (f, τ) ∈ R⁶; F_b is applied at B’s origin in B axes; at another frame F_c = Adᵀ_{g_bc}F_b; Fˢ = F_a is the spatial wrench and Fᵇ = F_b the body wrench.
atoms.feynman: A push-and-twist pair, which changes its description when you move where you measure it.
atoms.visual: Tile 🔧: a purple wrench slides to a new point growing its coral lever torque.

atoms.idea: Item 6: a wrench has a screw with pitch fᵀτ/‖f‖², axis through f×τ/‖f‖² along f (or along τ through 0), magnitude ‖f‖ (or ‖τ‖).
atoms.feynman: Every total push is one screwdriver.
atoms.visual: Tile 🔧 also shows Poinsot’s reduction to a single gold axis.

atoms.idea: Item 7 (start): F and V are reciprocal if F·V = 0; screws are reciprocal when their twist and wrench are. (Continues.)
atoms.feynman: Zero work means reciprocal.
atoms.visual: Tile 🔧 shows a power gauge at 0.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Summary items 7–8: reciprocal product S₁⊙S₂ = v₁·ω₂ + v₂·ω₁; a screw system’s dimension plus its reciprocal’s is 6; everything also works in the plane (Exercises 10–11). Bibliography: sources for twists and exponential coordinates; Ball and later screw-theory texts; Lie-group version in Appendix A.

atoms.idea: Item 7: the reciprocal product is S₁⊙S₂ = V₁·F₂ = v₁·ω₂ + v₂·ω₁; screws are reciprocal iff it is zero.
atoms.feynman: A fight-meter for bolts: zero means no fight.
atoms.visual: Tile 🔧: two 6-bar cards with swapped halves dot to 0 (lime).

atoms.idea: Item 8: a screw system is the span of S₁…S_k; its reciprocal system is all screws reciprocal to each Sᵢ; their dimensions sum to 6 in SE(3).
atoms.feynman: Every independent way of holding removes one of six ways of moving.
atoms.visual: Tile 🔧: the 6-cell purple/lime bar.

atoms.idea: All of these ideas carry over to planar motion (Exercises 10, 11).
atoms.feynman: Everything works on a flat tabletop too, just with fewer numbers.
atoms.visual: A 📄 tile links to the Flatland scene.

atoms.idea: Section 2.7 heading: Bibliography.

Sources: the geometric view of twists is credited to Paden; using exponential coordinates for robot motion is credited to Brockett, whose derivation also underpins Chapter 3; related classics are Ball and later screw-theory and kinematics texts (Hunt, Bottema & Roth, Duffy, Angeles, McCarthy); the abstract Lie-group version is Appendix A.
atoms.feynman: Every recipe in this chapter has a family tree of cooks behind it.
atoms.visual: Family-tree strip: 📜 Chasles/Poinsot (1800s) → 📚 Ball (1900) → 🔩 screw-theory texts → 💻 exponential coordinates for robots → 🦾 next chapter; tapping a node highlights which tile of the board it fed.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Exercises 1–5: vector identities; SE(3) group axioms; eigenstructure of ω̂ and R and the determinant formula; skew-matrix properties and so(3) as a 3-D vector space; Cayley’s rational parameterisation of SO(3).

atoms.idea: Section 2.8 heading: Exercises.

atoms.label: Ex 1
atoms.idea: Exercise 1: prove the triple-product swap a·(b×c) = (a×b)·c and the expansion a×(b×c) = (a·c)b − (a·b)c.
atoms.feynman: The volume of a box doesn’t care which pair of edges you cross first.
atoms.visual: Challenge mode in the rotation-matrix scene: drag three orange arrows a, b, c; two volume readouts (a·(b×c) and (a×b)·c) must match; for the second identity the learner drags coefficient sliders on b and c until the gold combination lands on a×(b×c), revealing the coefficients a·c and −a·b.

atoms.label: Ex 2
atoms.idea: Exercise 2: using 4×4 homogeneous matrices, verify SE(3) satisfies the group axioms under matrix multiplication.
atoms.feynman: Moves of a toy compose, undo and do-nothing just like Rubik’s cube moves.
atoms.visual: Challenge mode in the homogeneous scene: four badges (closure, identity, inverse, associativity) light only when the learner builds the right 4×4 products — e.g. must construct ḡ⁻¹ by hand (Rᵀ and −Rᵀp cells) so that ḡḡ⁻¹ = I.

atoms.label: Ex 3
atoms.idea: Exercise 3: for R = exp(ω̂θ): eigenvalues of ω̂ are 0, ±i (find eigenvectors); eigenvalues of R are 1, e^{±iθ} (the eigenvalue-1 vector is the axis); and det R = r₁ᵀ(r₂ × r₃).
atoms.feynman: The one direction a spinning top doesn’t move is its axle; every other direction goes round in circles.
atoms.visual: Challenge mode in the Rodrigues scene: learner drags a teal probe vector until R·probe lies exactly on top of the probe (lime) — it must find the axis; complex eigenvalues shown as dots on the unit circle at angles ±θ; a third task drags columns to make the signed volume +1.

atoms.label: Ex 4
atoms.idea: Exercise 4: prove R ω̂ Rᵀ = (Rω)^ and R(v×w) = Rv × Rw, and show the skew matrices form a 3-dimensional real vector space with an explicit basis.
atoms.feynman: Turning a spin is the spin of the turned axis; and every spin is a mix of three basic spins.
atoms.visual: Challenge mode in the rotation-matrix scene: (a) learner turns the camera until a conjugated hat grid matches a target; (b) build any given skew grid from three basis-spin sliders (x̂, ŷ, ẑ hat grids), proving dimension 3.

atoms.label: Ex 5
atoms.idea: Exercise 5 (Cayley parameters): show R_a = (I − â)⁻¹(I + â) is a rotation, verify its explicit entries (scaled by 1/(1+‖a‖²)), and recover a from a given R.
atoms.feynman: A recipe for turns that only uses adding and dividing — no sines or cosines needed.
atoms.visual: Challenge mode in the Euler-angles scene (“other 3-number maps”): drag an orange vector a; the body turns by the Cayley map; RᵀR and det badges stay lime; task: match a gold target pose by dragging a, and notice a must run to infinity for half-turns (coral).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Exercises 6–8: unit-quaternion group, rotating points by QXQ*, the 2-to-1 cover of SO(3), operation counts, the quaternion kinematic equation; degrees of freedom of a rigid body in Rⁿ; matrix exponential properties (begins).

atoms.label: Ex 6a
atoms.idea: Exercise 6(a): prove unit quaternions form a group under quaternion multiplication.
atoms.feynman: Combining two unit turns gives a unit turn; undoing is conjugating.
atoms.visual: Challenge mode in the quaternion scene: multiply two random unit quaternions and keep the lime ‖Q‖ = 1 ring lit; find the inverse by flipping the right bars.

atoms.label: Ex 6b
atoms.idea: Exercise 6(b): for a pure quaternion X = (0, x) and unit Q, QXQ* is pure with vector part (q₀² − q·q)x + 2q₀(q×x) + 2(x·q)q, which is the point x rotated by Q.
atoms.feynman: Sandwich the point between the turn and its mirror, and out pops the turned point.
atoms.visual: Challenge: a teal point x is sandwiched Q·X·Q*; three colored arrow terms build the result; learner adjusts Q to send x onto a gold target.

atoms.label: Ex 6c
atoms.idea: Exercise 6(c): unit quaternions double-cover SO(3): Q and −Q give the same rotation.
atoms.feynman: A belt held at both ends untwists only after two full turns.
atoms.visual: Challenge: find a second set of four bars (not the shown one) that produces the same pose — success when the learner flips all four signs.

atoms.label: Ex 6d
atoms.idea: Exercise 6(d): count additions and multiplications for composing/applying rotation matrices versus quaternions.
atoms.feynman: Which recipe uses fewer kitchen steps?
atoms.visual: Challenge: two operation counters tick as each method runs; learner predicts which is cheaper for composing (quaternion) and for applying to a vector (matrix) before revealing.

atoms.label: Ex 6e
atoms.idea: Exercise 6(e): a body spinning at unit rate about ω satisfies Q̇·Q* = (0, ω/2).
atoms.feynman: The quaternion spins at half speed — the half-angle shows up in the velocity too.
atoms.visual: Challenge: integrate Q̇ = ½(0, ω)·Q with small steps and keep the body glued to the exp(ω̂t) ghost; using ω instead of ω/2 makes it drift twice as fast (coral).

atoms.label: Ex 7
atoms.idea: Exercise 7: a rigid body in Rⁿ has ½(n + n²) degrees of freedom; split into translational (n) and rotational (n(n−1)/2).
atoms.feynman: A card on a table can slide two ways and turn one way; a ball in a room can slide three ways and turn three ways.
atoms.visual: Challenge mode in the frozen-distances scene: a dimension slider n = 2, 3, 4…; learner fills a bar with teal (translation) and orange (rotation-plane) cells; one orange cell per pair of axes, drawn as little planes.

atoms.label: Ex 8
atoms.idea: Exercise 8 (matrix exponential): with e^Λ = Σ Λᵏ/k! … (continues).
atoms.feynman: Keep doing a tiny step forever.
atoms.visual: Challenge setup in the Rodrigues scene: series bars for a general square matrix Λ.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Exercises 8–10: the matrix-exponential series converges, conjugation commutes with exp, and d/dt e^{Λθ} = Λθ̇e^{Λθ}; projection maps complete the proof of Prop 2.9; planar rotations SO(2) ≅ circle and exp on so(2).

atoms.label: Ex 8
atoms.idea: Exercise 8: (a) the series converges in some matrix norm; (b) g e^Λ g⁻¹ = e^{gΛg⁻¹}; (c) d/dt e^{Λθ} = (Λθ̇)e^{Λθ} = e^{Λθ}(Λθ̇).
atoms.feynman: The terms of the recipe get tiny so fast that the sum settles; changing your viewpoint before or after cooking gives the same dish.
atoms.visual: Challenge: a bar of term norms ‖Λᵏ‖/k! that must visibly shrink to 0 (factorial wins); a toggle compares g·exp(Λ)·g⁻¹ with exp(gΛg⁻¹) — learner chooses g to break it (impossible, always lime); a velocity arrow from finite differences matches Λθ̇·e^{Λθ}.

atoms.label: Ex 9
atoms.idea: Exercise 9: show image(ω̂) = ω⊥ and kernel(ω̂) = span ω; ωωᵀ and I − ωωᵀ are projections; I − e^{ω̂θ} is bijective on ω⊥ for θ ∈ (0, 2π); hence A = (I − e^{ω̂θ})ω̂ + ωωᵀθ is invertible.
atoms.feynman: Shine a light along the axis and across it: each piece of the machine only touches its own shadow, so nothing can cancel.
atoms.visual: Challenge mode in the twist scene: learner tries to find a non-zero teal v with A v = 0 by dragging; the along-axis and across-axis shadows of v (lime and slate) can never both vanish; projection sliders demonstrate P² = P.

atoms.label: Ex 10
atoms.idea: Exercise 10 (planar rotations): match SO(2) with points of the unit circle; for ω̂ = [0 −ω; ω 0], e^{ω̂θ} is the 2×2 rotation by ωθ; is exp: so(2) → SO(2) onto? one-to-one?
atoms.feynman: A clock hand is a point on a circle; winding a string around a spool shows many windings land on the same spot.
atoms.visual: Flatland scene: dial point on the unit circle drives the 2×2 grid; an exp slider winds a line (so(2)) around the circle — every point is hit (onto), many times (not one-to-one), shown as stacked ghost marks.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Exercises 10–12: in the plane, R ω̂ Rᵀ = ω̂; planar rigid motions SE(2), se(2) twists, their exponentials, pole of a planar motion, planar spatial/body velocities and the 3×3 adjoint; Rodrigues for non-unit ω.

atoms.label: Ex 10c
atoms.idea: Exercise 10(c): in 2-D, R ω̂ Rᵀ = ω̂ — planar rotations commute, so turning the viewpoint doesn’t change a planar spin.
atoms.feynman: A spinning record looks the same however you turn your head (as long as you stay above it).
atoms.visual: Flatland: rotate the camera; the spin readout ω is unchanged (lime).

atoms.label: Ex 11a
atoms.idea: Exercise 11 setup and (a): SE(2) as 3×3 [R p; 0 1], se(2) twists [ω̂ v; 0 0] with coordinates (v, ω) ∈ R³; show exp of a planar twist lies in SE(2), for ω = 0 and ω ≠ 0.
atoms.feynman: A card on a table: two slides and one turn, three knobs in all.
atoms.visual: Flatland challenge: three knobs (v_x, v_y teal, ω orange) and θ; the card flows along an arc or a line; learner must reach a gold card pose.

atoms.label: Ex 11b–c
atoms.idea: Exercise 11(b),(c): pure rotation about q is ξ = (q_y, −q_x, 1), pure translation is (v_x, v_y, 0); every planar motion is a pure rotation about a pole or a pure translation.
atoms.feynman: Any way you move a coaster on a table, you could have pinned it at one spot and turned it — unless you only slid it.
atoms.visual: Flatland challenge: drop two card poses; the learner drags a gold pin until spinning about it carries card 1 onto card 2; the true pole lights lime; parallel cards show a slide instead.

atoms.idea: Exercise 12: verify the Rodrigues formula for non-unit ω (rescale by ‖ω‖).

atoms.idea: Exercise 13: for a screw twist ξ_a in frame A, (a) its coordinates in B are Ad_{g_ab}⁻¹ ξ_a = Ad_{g_ba} ξ_a; (b) moving the screw by g gives ξ′_a = Ad_g ξ_a, still in A.

atoms.idea: Exercise 14: show (Ad_g)⁻¹ = Ad_{g⁻¹} and Ad_{g₁g₂} = Ad_{g₁}Ad_{g₂}.

pages.summary: Exercises 16–18: spatial and body velocity of the 2-DOF arm (optionally with a symbolic package, Appendix B); frame invariance of the reciprocal product, reciprocal bases for zero- and infinite-pitch screws, dependence of three parallel coplanar revolute screws; the hybrid velocity (ṗ, ωˢ) (begins).

atoms.label: Ex 16b–d
atoms.idea: Exercise 16(b)–(d): find the spatial and body velocities of the end frame in terms of the joint angles and their rates; optionally check via the spatial velocity of C3’s origin; a symbolic package (Appendix B) helps.
atoms.feynman: How fast is the lamp head moving, from the room’s view and from the head’s own view?
atoms.visual: Challenge: learner sets two twist columns (one per joint); the 🌍 and 🧍 bars computed from their answer must match the measured ones while θ̇₁, θ̇₂ knobs are wiggled.

atoms.label: Ex 17a–b
atoms.idea: Exercise 17(a),(b): an operator is frame invariant if it doesn’t depend on the frame; show the reciprocal product is frame invariant but the plain twist inner product is not.
atoms.feynman: The fight between two bolts doesn’t depend on who is watching; the naive dot product of their recipe cards does.
atoms.visual: Challenge mode in the reciprocal scene: drag the observer frame around; the ⊙ readout stays frozen (lime) while a naive V₁·V₂ readout wanders (coral).

atoms.label: Ex 17c–d
atoms.idea: Exercise 17(c),(d): build bases for everything reciprocal to (i) a pure hinge screw through a point and (ii) a pure sliding screw, and explain each basis element geometrically (a clever frame choice helps).
atoms.feynman: Which motions never fight a hinge? Which never fight a drawer?
atoms.visual: Challenge: given one gold screw, the learner places five independent ghost screws that all keep the power gauge at 0 (e.g. lines through the hinge axis, pure translations perpendicular to the drawer).

atoms.label: Ex 17e
atoms.idea: Exercise 17(e): prove that three hinge screws lying parallel in one plane are linearly dependent, by finding four independent screws reciprocal to every one of them.
atoms.feynman: Three parallel hinges in a row can’t block more than two ways of moving.
atoms.visual: Challenge: three parallel gold hinge lines in a plane; the dimension bar must show 4 lime cells, not 3 — learner finds the fourth reciprocal screw.

atoms.idea: Exercise 18(c)–(e): hybrid velocity is independent of the spatial frame’s position but not its orientation, and of the body frame’s orientation but not its position; interpret wrenches in hybrid coordinates and their change-of-frame rules.
